maintopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND STATUS OF ALIENS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 20, respecting citizenship, nationality, naturalization and status of aliens.
He said: In view of the importance of the bill it is felt desirable to make a preliminary statement which will be helpful in explaining its general provisions and which will also assist hon. members in their deliberations of it.
On May 24 of this year, speaking in Winnipeg, the Prime Minister remarked on the fact that one of the symbols of nationhood that is lacking in Canada at present is a clearly defined nationality or citizenship status. He indicated that it would be his intention, if the government were returned, to have that defect remedied. The present bill is designed to achieve that purpose.
It should not be concluded from this that the bill in reality makes any sweeping change or that there has not previously been any such thing as Canadian nationality. Despite what one often hears to the contrary, there has been a Canadian nationality, but the difficulty has been that the existing definitions were so specialized and so unrelated that they led to a condition of great confusion and misunderstanding. "Canadian nationals" have hitherto been defined under the Canadian Nationals Act, but in reality the definition had virtually no significance. The term "Canadian citizen" is now, in strict accuracy, only an immigration status. As a third type of status, there is that of "British subject". Undoubtedly each of us in this house is all three of these, but I venture with great respect to suggest that few of us know what it means when the words "Canadian citizen" are used at the present time, or how that status differs from "Canadian national". If we do not know, what chance has the ordinary citizen of this country to know what he is? Sometimes he is told that he is a Canadian and should be proud of it. And then he comes to fill in some form asking his national status and is told that there is no such thing as "Canadian". It is extremely undesirable that there should be confusion about so fundamental a matter.
I have referred to the need for clearer definition of national status in this country. An equally great need, in clarifying the definition, 47696-85
is to remove a large number of legal complications that arise under existing legislation. As I have said, we have at present a naturalization act that defines British subjects and governs naturalization of aliens in Canada. We have also "Canadian Nationals" Act which defines "Canadian nationals". [DOT] Thirdly, we have The Immigration Act, which defines Canadian citizens for purposes of immigration entry. At present a person may be a British subject by naturalization in Canada, but he may have no right of entry because he is not a Canadian citizen. This arises if he has been out of Canada long enough to have lost his "domicile" under the Immigration Act, and the resulting situation is an unending source of difficulty, confusion and embarrassment for Canadians who have gone abroad. Similarly, a person who is the son of Canadian parents, and who is a British subject and a Canadian national may, in certain circumstances, find that he, too, is not a Canadian citizen and cannot enter Canada. For example, if Canadians go abroad and have a child abroad, that child is a "Canadian national", but he is not a "Canadian citizen" for purposes of the Immigration Act, and so he has no right to come into the country. A Canadian national who cannot enter the very country of which he is a national! It is even possible for a Canadian national not to be a British subject. Whether any case of this type has actually occurred I do not know, but due to requirements of registration under the Naturalization Act which do not exist under the Canadian Nationals Act, such a thing can occur.
Mr. Speaker, as a result, to remove all this confusion it is the intention of the government to undertake an extensive revision of the present Naturalization Act in terms of Canadian citizenship. By this I mean that the bill I am introducing is in reality a comprehensive amendment of .the Naturalization Act in which, to avoid the old sources of confusion, all definitions, conditions and qualifications are in terms of a general status of "Canadian citizen". Further to remove difficulty, the Canadian Nationals Act will be repealed and its whole purpose will be encompassed in this new bill. Along with this it is intended to amend the Immigration Act so as to alter its present definitions and provide that anyone who is a Canadian citizen under this new bill will automatically and at all times have a right of entry into Canada. If this is carried through, the result will be that in future there will be only one act governing all aspects and all practical consequences of national status in Canada.

speechtext: Canadian Citizenship

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
We will thus achieve a new status of "Canadian citizen" which will be an inclusive and definitive status. At the same time, I want to emphasize and make clear that this will not remove from anyone who now has it, nor eliminate for persons born or naturalized in future, the status of British subject. A Canadian who is now a British subject will under this act continue to be a British subject. A person who is hereafter born a Canadian citizen will thereby also be a British subject. An alien who comes to Canada and is naturalized as a Canadian citizen will similarly become a British subject. The change will be in removing the confusion of conflicting and unrelated definitions that we now have. So far as Canada is concerned the dominant fact will be that of being a Canadian citizen. With it, as a correlative, and important in the commonwealth as a whole, each will also have the status of British subject.
Without going into the details of the bill, there are a few important aspects that it seems desirable to mention. I have said that in general substance, the bill is a broad revision of the Naturalization Act done in terms of Canadian citizenship. It first of all defines who are Canadian citizens by birth. It next sets forth the qualifications for naturalization as a Canadian citizen, and these again are essentially the same as those now m force. There is one additional difference, however, that should be noted. In future, non-Canadian British subjects will be required to take out papers before becoming Canadian citizens. This may appear to be a fundamental change, but it is a change more in procedure than in substance. At present a non-Canadian British subject has no right of entry into Canada, and he does not become a "Canadian citizen" under the Immigration Act until he has had domicile here for five years. In essence all that is now being required is that in future the change of status to Canadian citizenship shall be marked by the acquisition of formal papers. It is felt that this will be a decided advantage to the individuals concerned, as it will give greater certainty and security to their position for purposes of diplomatic protection abroad and of immigration entry when they come to our borders.
I might say that the war has shown the importance of having basic documents for prima facie proof of national status. There have been thousands of cases where persons abroad have appealed to our representatives or to the protecting power for aid on the ground that they were Canadians. Persons born in Canada have been able to produce
fMr. Martin.]
birth certificates, thus supplying a basis for proof. Others naturalized in Canada have been able to produce naturalization certificates. But persons who came to Canada from other parts of the commonwealth have had nothing whatever to show that they 'had become Canadian citizens and were the responsibility of the Canadian government. In peace time there have been similar cases of confusion, difficulty and real hardship. For this reason, it is important to provide papers for non-Canadian British subjects who become Canadian citizens.
On the subject of naturalization I might mention one change that is important throughout the bill. In the past, "married women" have been classed with minors, lunatics, and idiots as persons under a disability. They could not become naturalized or control their national status as independent persons except in very special circumstances. The government looks upon this as an anachronism that has no place to-day and all disabilities for married women have been eliminated in the present bill.
With regard to loss of Canadian citizenship, the conditions are the same as those at present for the loss of the status of British subject- with one addition. That addition is the insertion of a provision for automatic loss of citizenship by a naturalized person who stays out of Canada for six years or more, unless he comes within one of the specified classes or takes steps to protect his citizenship. The provision does not apply to naturalized persons who have served in our armed forces. In addition there are exceptions for naturalized persons who are abroad in the service of Canada, or for a Canadian corporation or business concern, or to go to university, or for reasons of ill health, and so forth. Hitherto there has been a provision for revocation of British subject status if a naturalized person has been absent for seven years. However, it is impossible to keep track of persons who are absent so as to know how long they have been away, and many whose naturalization should have been revoked have remained British subjects. In this war we have had such persons crop up; for example, Germans naturalized in Canada who returned to Germany in 1933 or 1934, whose absence was not known, and who now claim protection and benefits as Canadians. In many cases there is every reason to suspect that a great number of these people were ardent nazis and complete Germans during the war, .however Canadian they may now profess to feel. In future, with the passage of this bill, this will not happen. If such people are absent from Canada for six years or more and do not protect their

citizenship and are not in the excepted classes, they will automatically cease to be Canadians. Before concluding, there are two sections of the bill which I should like to mention particularly. Both are new; neither introduces any change in substantive law; yet I think they may be of considerable significance to people who become naturalized in Canada. One section authorizes the Secretary of State, with the approval of the governor in council, to take measures-
-to provide facilities to enable applicants for certificates of citizenship to receive instruction in the responsibilities and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
The other provides that the courts, in conducting naturalization proceedings-
-shall, by appropriate ceremonies, impress upon applicants the responsibilities and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
I think that hitherto we have not paid sufficient attention to these matters. In many cases people have become naturalized without having any real consciousness of the fact that they were taking a very significant, step, and sometimes without a true understanding of the obligations incurred. Apart from the purely legal consequences of acquiring a new citizenship, we must remember that in a democracy there are obligations and responsibilities upon a citizen, and these should be carefully explained, it is thought, to those who join us, and they should be fully impressed with the nature of the undertaking. They should also foe given some understanding, in a helpful and cooperative way, of how government in Canada works, and of the great traditions of constitutional liberty and even justice that are the root and source of our individual liberty. We are too apt to take these things for granted, even after a frightful war that has shown us they must be cherished and fought for bitterly if they are to'be preserved; and we should take care that every new citizen becomes a doughty champion of the democratic way of life.
Closely related to this, and yet distinct, is the desirability of making every new citizen feel that he is truly becoming part of Canada. Our "new Canadians" bring to this country much that is rich and good, and in Canada they find a new way of life and new hope for the future. They should all be made to feel that they, like the rest of us, are Canadians, citizens of a great country, guardians of proud traditions and trustees of all that is best in life for generations of Canadians yet to be. For the national unity of Canada and for the future and greatness of this country it is felt to be of the utmost importance that all of us, new Canadians or old, have a consciousness of a common purpose and common inter-47696

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I move that the following resolution be referred to the committee on external affairs:
That this house do approve of the convention concerning the protection against accidents of workers employed in loading or unloading ships (revised), which was adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations at its sixteenth session in Geneva on the 27th day of April, 1932.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday evening the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) expressed doubt as to whether this matter should go to the external affairs committee or to the industrial relations committee. The acting leader of the government on that occasion intimated that this matter had received a considerable amount of thought from the government, and that it was considered that it. should go to the external affairs committee. At the time the question was raised in the house I felt the hon. member for Peel had made a point worthy of further consideration. During the week-end I have read carefully the proposed agreement, and in my opinion it is going to the wrong committee. In its subject matter it deals almost exclusively with matters relating to labour- the conditions under which seamen shall operate and shall be protected in the loading and unloading of ships. The next resolution on the order paper has to do with the conditions among miners, and there is reference to safety devices for both classes of w'orkers.
While it is true that this is in the form of an international agreement as between ourselves and the international labour organization, and therefore with other governments who will adhere to the agreement, the subject matter is not one which in my opinion should' properly' be considered by the external affairs committee. That would be the wrong committee. In appointing the external affairs committee the whips, who discussed the matter with the various political parties in the house, arranged the membership not on the basis of a knowledge of safety devices at sea or safety devices in the mines, but on the 
basis of interest in the external relations of this country and all that that involves. To refer this matter to the external affairs committee places in the hands of members, who may be quite qualified to go into these matters, something which is not of primary interest to that, committee. On the other hand it denies to those whose principal interest is in industrial affairs of this description the right to go through the agreement and approve or disapprove it, section by section. I believe that in referring it to the external affairs committee we are making a mistake.
I am a member of that committee, but when I read the agreement I realized that there are colleagues of mine who are not on the committee, but who are eminently well qualified to discuss this matter. For instance, throughout the whole of his life the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has been a miner. While he is not on the external affairs committee, he is on the committee dealing with industrial relations. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who lives by the sea, knows something at least about ships and seamen, and the conditions under which they work. He may or may not be on the external affairs committee; I have forgotten. In any event in my view this matter should go before the committee on industrial relations, and my suggestion is that in this respect the proposal be reconsidered.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I have only two comments to make respecting this resolution. In the first place, let us not forget that it has been unearthed from the old league of nations stuff. It will be noted that the agreement is dated 1932. It reminds me of the old social legislation, cooked by Herridge and Finlayson for Bennett, that parliament had to swallow during the session of 1935.	'
This is called a convention. It is not a convention at all. It is in the same class as the blank forms for the code of civil procedure. It was drafted by the nonentities who adorned the league of nations in Geneva, and who attempted to justify its existence at the expense of all countries, including Canada, which had to pay so much each year, even during the war, when the league of nations was inoperative. It is a humbug, from beginning to end. It is a kind of petty humbug-and that is h-u-m-b-u-g. It is supposedly to help labour, but it will not help labour a bit.
This agreement will not settle the difficulties of labour. Of that we have evidence rigjht now in British ports, where stevedores have been on strike for over a month. Has this

Labour-Approval oj Convention
been accepted by England? This is the kind of so-called unilateral convention which was so roundly ridiculed by the late Mr. Cahan, while he was a member of the house-although after he was made a minister he swallowed it. He could not digest it after his party was defeated at the polls.
This convention is called unilateral-and 'why?' Not because it has been made by two parties, as all conventions are. All conventions are supposed to be bilateral. It has been made by a bunch of fools and parasites who were over there at Geneva-those public exploiters and others, who were preparing stuff to justify the payment of exorbitant salaries and other exorbitant fees for travelling and other expenses. They are parasites, that is all.
Here we are, solemnly accepting the convention. Let us see why. I have great respect for labour, but I have none for those people. My respect is for the real labouring man, not for those with gold chains as big as my fist and cigars as long as from here to to-morrow. What is this international labour organization? They are all these fellows who live on the fat of the land and who call themselves labour men. They are just parasites. They are just people who cannot work and they call themselves labour men. They go through the world with schemes like this; [DOT] they sell their goods and they find people who are credulous enough to believe that they are promoting the welfare of the working men, that they are doing so much for the working men. We are asked to adopt this convention which is not a convention and cannot possibly be a convention. We are asked to do this for the sake of the working men.
Let us consider this from another point of view. I have said something of what I think of those soft brains of Geneva, those international fakers. I will now come to brass tacks and facts. The whole world was in consternation upon learning of the monster strike of stevedores in the ports of Great Britain. We have reduced our rations of perishable food to the utmost in the hope that it will benefit mankind, that it will benefit Europeans who are starving and who need foodstuffs from the two producing countries which can send any overseas, Canada and the United States. My information is that a large quantity of perishable food has rotted on the ships in British ports because these stevedores are on strike and have not realized their duties as human citizens to help in unloading this stuff, which perhaps would have saved the lives not only of children but of undernourished older people. We are trying to do something for the labour men, including these stevedores, and yet they 47696-S6J
refuse to carry out their duties, duties which none of us would refuse to carry out if we were in their position.
Some strikes are stupid, but this strike is criminal. Although the government of Great Britain at the present time is a Labour government, it must be very weak if it has not found means to see to it that these men return at once to their jobs to fulfil a duty which is undoubtedly a national duty. I have some questions which will appear on the order paper to-morrow concerning the shipment of perishable goods to ports in the United Kingdom after this strike .had been declared. I am asking what happened to the perishable food that was on the ships.	.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
know that at the present time the ships are being unloaded by troops?

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
I know that troops are
working, but they have had no experience at stevedoring. They were called in at the last moment. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar knows that the troops were called in after much food had rotted and was of no use to anyone. I appreciate the fact that the troops are there, but what I cannot understand is that the government in Great Britain has not been able to make this class of .labouring men understand that they have an obligation to fulfil, a national duty in time of emergency.
Hostilities have ceased, but victory has not yet been won. Victory will be won only when there is order in society. We shall not have victory until these men realize that they have a duty to do the work they are experienced in doing, to do all they can to- unload this food for the' benefit of the people of the old country. Not only that; I am informed that even though this strike has been declared, perishable food shipped from Canada and destined for Europe is still being directed to British ports instead of being sent direct to the ports of Europe where there is no such criminal strike. If that is the situation, I hope it will be corrected immediately.
In my humble view we should not be asked to have an academic discussion of the work of a man who is not a labour man, but who claims to be, or the work of a group of men who claim to be labour men just for the sake of propaganda. I have seem Jouhaux, the French labour leader, who is just an exploiter of the man in overalls, who is just an exploiter of public opinion. There are many other things that are more important than this for labour, and one is the freedom of labour, the right of labour to ehoose leaders who are not affiliated with international organizations.
At the present time labour men who belong to associations which are affiliated

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
No, I do not think so. I concede much that my hon. friend has said. The resolution has industrial aspect, but undoubtedly it does have international implications, and since it is concerned with external affairs I believe it should be referred to the appropriate committee.
I must make reference to the most unfortunate speech delivered by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I believe that the international labour organization, which was a part of the old league of nations organization, has been one of the finest and noblest forces for good in this world in the last twenty years. As one who has taken a deep
interest in it and in the labour movement all my life and has had the privilege of attending some of the meetings of the international labour organization in Canada during the last few years I wish to say that they have justified themselves abundantly by the work they have done in the service of the common man in this and other countries. It is not for us here to condemn them for the sake of passing applause for humorous references. We should admire the work that they have done.
Surely this is the democratic way, to refer this matter to a committee of this house, representing the Progressive Conservatives, the C.C.F., the Social Crediters, the Independents, I believe, and the government, to make such a report as in their judgment they see fit to make to this house.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, as I have indicated, would have been right in making his suggestion last year, but now that we have acceded to his suggestion and that of the hon. leader of the opposition and set up a committee on external affairs, this resolution should properly be sent to that committee for its consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
I am not rising to discuss the
relative merits of the proposals as to which of these two committees this resolution should be referred to. With all deference, I doubt if that is of very serious consequence to the house, because they are both good committees. I am rising however to make one or two brief observations and to ask three questions which I think are pertinent. I assume that the hon. member who introduced the resolution will have something to say before it passes.
The resolution asks approval of the international labour organization convention No. 32 regarding prevention of accidents in the loading and unloading of ships. With that objective, I am sure, every hon. member in this house will be in accord. I had thought the minister would make some further comment with regard to the approval of the convention before asking that it be sent to the committee, and I hope he will do that, because eveiy hon. member would like to know more about it before the reference to a committee is made.
Why has the government's approval of this convention been delayed for thirteen years? Is there anything objectionable about it which would account for its not having been brought forward before this? I am informed that the draft convention was passed at Geneva in 1032. and the question. I

Labour-Approval oj Convention
repeat, is this: Why has the approval of this convention been -delayed so long? I am inclined to agree largely with the remarks of the minister who just sat down as to the work the organization has tried to do, but it raises another question. I am informed that during the last quarter of a century some sixty-seven conventions have been passed by this international labour organization and that- only nine have been approved by this parliament. I would ask the minister to give us some idea as to why. if this organization enjoys all the prestige it appears to do, so few of its conventions have been brought to this house for approval.
I understand that during that twenty-five years Canada has sent delegates to every meeting, or practically every meeting, that has been held. I would ask the minister to tell us how much money Canada has contributed to the international labour organization in that time and how much it is contributing annually now. I ask that for the information of the public. It is possible that most members of the house know the answers to these questions, but I think the great mass of the people of Canada do not understand why so few of these conventions have been brought here for our approval.
There are two other, minor, questions with respect to procedure upon which the minister might enlighten us. Is there anything in this convention which the dominion government, under the constitution as it now exists, has no power to carry out? If so, what is the government's thought as to how these objectives might be met?
The other question of secondary importance is this:	What procedure will the government follow after this resolution is approved, in order to make the convention effective in Canada ?
Let me say before I sit down that we on this side of the house have every intention of supporting the objective of this resolution. We shall be interested to know, and we hope the government will make clear in the committee, the implications of all the details in the many articles of the convention- Generally the resolution will have our support.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext:
Like the leader of the opposition, I have been wondering why this resolution was not brought down long ago, in view of the fact that the convention was passed in 1932. I believe, as does the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that the resolution is being sent to the wrong committee. With all deference to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), I was going to say that probably

he had not read the resolution over carefully, though I know he has. Every clause, every article in it deals strictly with labour or labour relations. It deals with hours of work, with the amount of wages, and with the entire income of the worker. With the resolution which follows, these conventions deal with almost every branch of labour, from the work around shipyards to agriculture, mining and practically every phase of labour. Nowhere do they touch upon international relations except as the labour relations of one nation apply to another, which is very small in comparison with the general labour situation.
The leader of the opposition said that he would support this, and he did not think it made much material difference which committee it went to. Then he went on to point out'that the government should give us much more information about the resolution before referring it to a small number of men from this house. That is the very point that I would call to your attention, Mr. Speaker. The very fact that this resolution will be referred to but, a small number of men chosen from this house is the reason why it should go to the committee that deals with these problems. When the committee on industrial relations was set up, every party, I believe, had the same thought in mind as the Social Credit party, that those men were picked because they were more closely connected with labour, and had possibly a better knowledge of labour relations than some of the others.
I am not saying that hon. members are not all equally interested in labour problems, but there are some men who are more closely related to the different problems confronting labour, and in my opinion the men on the industrial relations committee have a better knowledge of labour relations than those who are on the external affairs committee.
With all respect to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I suggest that he should give serious consideration to the whole question. I would be against having this resolution passed on to the committee on external affairs. I have no objections to its being turned over to the committee on industrial relations. Before this resolution passes there should be some marked changes in it. There are fundamental principles involved. The question still presents itself, what good it will do us in Canada? I believe we should spend our time, and possibly we could do so to greater advantage, applying all our resources and our energies to the solution of our own labour problems before undertaking to go abroad in an attempt to solve great international labour problems. In other words, we should put our own house in order first. Notwithstanding that, however, I have no

Labour-Approval of Convention
objections to having the matter referred to a committee, though I think it should be sent to the proper committee, and tjiat is the committee on industrial relations and not the committee on external affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: APPROVAL OK CONVENTION CONCERNING PROTECTION AGAINST ACCIDENTS OF WORKERS LOADING OR UNLOADING SHIPS
speechtext: I thought the passing of this resolution would be a matter of form. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) spoke about these conventions. We have adopted, I think, about nine conventions. I can give the names if the house wishes. But many of the conventions adopted by the international labour organization come within provincial jurisdiction. What happens is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs notifies the provincial legislatures of their passage. I wish to join with my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) in the statement he made. Some very important things have been said to-day about the international labour organization. I think many of them have been said in ignorance, if I may say so in a kindly way.

speechtext:
It is meant to be kindly. Of the organizations that had their birth in international relations after the last war, I know of none that has made a greater contribution to the well-being of the working men and women in this world than the international labour organization. I have been an advocate of the I.L.O. ever since its inception. It was the brain child of Sam Gompers, who was president of the American Federation of Labour. If my memory serves me rightly, Sir Robert Borden had a great deal to do with the fashioning of the charter, if you wish to call it a charter.
All this does, Mr. Speaker, is merely to ratify the convention which was complied with in the passing of the Canada Shipping Act in 1934. To my hon. friend who spoke so fervently about the terms of the convention I suggest that he study the Canada Shipping Act and see if it does conform to the articles laid down in this convention.
What my hon. friend the leader of the opposition says is quite true. I think this convention might have been ratified long ago, at the time the resolution was introduced in 1939 by the late Hon. Mr. Rogers, who was then Minister of Labour. I am given to understand that through some error it was not ratified by this house.
So far as I am concerned there are arguments on both sides as to whether it should go to the industrial relations committee or to the external affairs committee, as has been suggested by the government.
For the information of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) I should like to say that the I.L.O. is meeting in Paris at the present time. The Canadian delegate was at one time a member of this house. Mr. Bengough, the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, is a member of the governing body. Mr. MacNamara, my deputy, is also a member. I hope that the I.L.O. will be strengthened and that this agency for the study of questions on an international basis affecting working conditions in the broader sense will make the same contribution in years to come that it has in the past.
I should like to correct the impression of one hon. member who said that he would like the bill to pass. This is not a bill; it is merely ratification of a convention, which is covered by the Canada Shipping Act and the setting up of the necessary machinery to carry out the provisions of this particular convention.
I am sorry I cannot speak from memory about the costs, but I shall be glad to obtain the information and give it to my hon. friend some time later this afternoon.

Resolved, that this house do approve of the convention concerning statistics of wages and hours of work in the principal mining and manufacturing industries, including building and construction and ini agriculture, which was adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization of the league of nations at its twenty-fourth session in Geneva, on the 20th day of June, 1938,-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you put the question I should like to make a few comments. I know I have no right to refer to the discussion that took place' on the other resolution, but with due respect, the minister did not answer one or two of my questions. One of them can be asked on this resolution. If we ratify this convention, has the dominion

power to carry out what we are doing, or does some of the jurisdiction fall to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION CONCERNING STATISTICS OF WAGES AND HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE
speechtext: May I answer my hon. friend now? The dominion is already carrying out, through the bureau of statistics, the provisions of this convention. It prepares statistics on hours of labour, wages, and related matters. It is being carried out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION CONCERNING STATISTICS OF WAGES AND HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE
speechtext: There is one other question that perhaps it will be in order to ask at this time. I understand that under the constitution of the international labour organization this government is under an obligation to submit conventions and recommendations to the national legislatures. That is the way the phraseology came to me from the organization in Montreal. If that is the constitutional position, how is it that few of those sixty-seven conventions have been referred to this parliament over the past twenty-five years? Why should there have been only nine, rather than more?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION CONCERNING STATISTICS OF WAGES AND HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I thought I had
answered my hon. friend; at least I tried to answer him. He appreciates, as I do, the constitutional implications in labour legislation in Canada. Certain things come purely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, while others of course have national implications. It is to my knowledge that in the case of conventions which affect provincial jurisdiction or legislation, the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Secretary of State informs the provincial governments. That is why more of these conventions have not been adopted by this parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION CONCERNING STATISTICS OF WAGES AND HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Then might I be permitted to add one other word. In our inquiries with respect to the work of this organization, of which we very much approve, wo find that of these sixty-seven conventions, while Canada has dealt with only nine, practically every other country has dealt with many more. My information is that Belgium has dealt with thirty-three, Denmark with nineteen, France with thirty-one, Norway with twenty-three, Sweden with twenty-five, Switzerland with fifteen, the United Kingdom with thirty-four, Australia with twelve and New Zealand with twenty-three. The only reason I am raising this point is that if we are to continue to make considerable financial contributions to this organization we ought to pay more attention to their recommendations.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION CONCERNING STATISTICS OF WAGES AND HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRY AND AGRICULTURE

Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs):	My hon. friend was good
enough to send me notice of his question
Public Works-Tenders

earlier in the day. My reply is that a change has taken place in the matter of hospital facilities for this department in the Montreal area. In addition to Ste. Anne's hospital, which makes provision for over one thousand beds, we had planned to build a new hospital with four hundred active treatment beds on what is known as the Benny farm on Sherbrooke street, to be known as the Currie Memorial hospital. We now find it necessary to defer this programme, for. the reason that in all probability the army is going to turn over to us the main part of the Montreal military hospital, making provision for five hundred active treatment beds. Since this gives us more beds than construction of the new hospital on the Benny farm would have provided, there is no justification at this time for our proceeding with the new construction on the Benny farm.
However, we do need hospital facilities for tubercular cases, and hope to erect or acquire in the near future a permanent five hundred-bed sanatorium in the Montreal area for patients from the province of Quebec. We are also preceding with the erection of a health and occupational centre at Senneville, near Ste. Anne's. This will provide for 180 patients, and will be a most modern plant for the practise of this new type of treatment known as physical medicine, whereby veterans, after they no longer need active treatment, are restored to health and full recovery of their functions in healthful and congenial environment and conditions.

speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Public Works. Is it a regulation of this department to call for tenders before letting out contracts? speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PUBLIC WORKS
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN CALLING FOR TENDERS AND LETTING CONTRACTS
speechtext:
In the Department of Public Works it is the practice to call for tenders either in the erection of buildings or other kinds of work. Generally such calls for tenders appear in the press, and no one is barred from tendering. The general practice has been that the lowest bidder receives the contract. Of course there have been some exceptions to that rule. I recall one occasion in British Columbia where, after calling for 
tenders, and finding we could not get bids, we had to come to an agreement with a firm to do the work. However the general practice is to ask publicly for tenders, the lowest bidder getting the contract.

Mr. HO"WE: This bill is designed to place Trans-Canada Air Lines in a position to undertake the substantially increased responsibilities which will be placed1 upon it during the next few years, as a result of the extension and improvement of existing Canadian air services and the establishment of new Canadian air services particularly in the international field. Trans-Canada Air Lines has been designated by the government to operate all services of a main line character within Canada and to operate Canadian international air services. To carry out this task it must be in a. position to multiply its activities several times over. At the same time it must be ready and able to act in a flexible fashion; for the development of civil aviation has been,

Trans-Canada Air Lines
and is likely to continue at such a rapid rate that present conditions governing particular air operations are likely to require substantial modification as development takes place from year to year. The purpose of this bill is, therefore', to provide a broad framework acceptable to parliament, within which Trans-Canada Air Lines under the supervision of the minister responsible for civil aviation, and with the approval of the governor in council can meet any contingency that may arise in carrying out the duties allotted to it.
Trans-Canada Air Lines, a relatively new organization, established by statute in 1937, has already established a record of which the Canadian people may be proud. Its regular commercial operations now extend from the west coast to the east coast and on to Newfoundland. ' It is also operating a non-commercial wartime service for the government across the north Atlantic which in due course will be transformed into an- ordinary commercial line. Its achievements have been such that Canada's reputation among other countries in the field of commercial aviation has been substantially enhanced.
It is the intention of the government to continue to develop Canadian air services, domestic [DOT] and external, in a manner commensurate with our needs and with the preeminent position which we hold in the field of air transport. We do not propose any exaggerated pattern of growth merely for reasons of prestige, or any forced expansion out of line with our normal economic and national needs. Compared with the programmes of some otheT countries our own plans appear reasonable and even modest; nevertheless they do involve the addition of many thousands of route miles to our existing network of services.
Within the domestic field some of our plans for development of main line services have already been announced. New four-motor aircraft are to be provided before many months and a shorter transcontinental service across the great lakes is to be initiated. Other main line services are to be added, including for example, a service from Winnipeg through Saskatoon to Edmonton. The studies which are at present being carried on with a view to-elaborating the-new main line services which Trans-Canada Air .Lines should establish are not yet complete, but as this' work progresses it is my intention to keep this house fully informed of our plans for domestic, development by T.C.A.
In addition, we have been granted certain new rights for air services from Canada to the United States. T.C.A. is already operating the only through service from Toronto to New York. Under the new agreement with the United States signed last February, Trans-Canada Air Lines will establish additional services from Halifax to Boston, from Toronto to Cleveland, from Toronto to Chicago, from the lake head to Duluth, from Victoria to Seattle, and from Whitehorse to Fairbanks.
These new services to the United States together with the new services which Trans-Canada Air Lines will establish within Canada will in all likelihood more than double the present route mileage operated by T.C.A.
In addition we propose, subject to satisfactory agreements with the other countries concerned and after we have acquired suitable new equipment and more trained personnel, to initiate three main international services; the first across the north Atlantic to the United Kingdom; the second from eastern Canada to the West Indies and Caribbean area and Latin America; and the third, a trans-Pacific route which will be operated ' in cooperation with other commonwealth services in that area. Decision has not yet been reached whether our Canadian air operations in the Pacific will extend as far as the antipodes or whether they will connect at an intermediate point with other commonwealth services from the far east and Australia.
It will take some time to make the necessary arrangements for these services and to get them established on a regular basis. In all probability a period of two or three years may elapse before the pattern is complete, although we hope that a regular commercial service on the north Atlantic will be in full operation before many weeks have passed. In any event, the establishment of these new international routes will involve route mileage that will probably be close to five times the present mileage operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines in North America. To sum up then, the addition of new mainline services within Canada, of new services to the United States, and of new international services will probably multiply Trans-Canada Air Lines present route mileage five or six times over. This full development will obviously require substantial additions to the capital, equipment and personnel of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
I have already said that I do not consider these plans extravagant. Admittedly, there must be a substantial financial backing to get them started, but the whole intention of the Canadian government in developing this pattern has been primarily to develop services which have a reasonable chance of operating on an economic basis; and not for the sake
Trans-Canada Air Lines

of national prestige to embark upon useless operations which will require continuation for an indefinite period of costly subsidies.
However, to place Trans-Canada Air Lines in a position to undertake all these services, a substantial increase in its capital is necessary. (Its present capitalization of $5,000,000 is adequate for its present operations but does not leave any leeway.) Accordingly the bill proposes an increase in the capital of Trans-Canada Air Lines to $25,000,000 which we believe will be adequate to provide for implementation of the plans which I have described.
Further, special administrative arrangements are necessary in connection with major international air operations. Services to the United States are really part of our domestic network and have always been considered as natural transfrontier extensions of domestic services. These particular services accordingly will be operated directly by Trans-Canada Air Lines. The long through international air services, however, will have to be treated as separate entities for both administrative and operational reasons. Not only do these long international operations differ considerably in nature from our domestic operations but each of them differs from the other in regard to operating conditions, distances, types of traffic and similar matters. For this reason it is desirable to separate them from the domestic network while at the same time utilizing the advantages that can be obtained through the training, experience and high standards that have characterized the domestic operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Moreover, we, along with other nations who are members of the provisional international civil aviation organization now functioning in Montreal have accepted the obligation to present full details on each of our international air operations to the organization so that they may maintain a complete register of operating and cost statistics of each international air service.
There are also definite advantages in an administrative organization for international lines which will permit segregation of all statistical detail, financial and otherwise for each of our major international operations; otherwise we may become confused between them and may not always have a clear picture of the value and position of each.
For these reasons it is believed that a separate company or companies should be established for operation of the major international air lines which we will plan to establish. We have not yet reached the stage in our planning where it is possible to state whether a single company will be sufficient for this 
purpose or whether more than one will be required; it is likely however that differences in operating conditions will require more than one company.
We have decided and announced that Trans-Canada Air Lines-, the government-owned Canadian Air service will 'be charged with the operation of our international services. There is a definite advantage in providing common supervision and common standards for all government-owned air services and in achieving an integrated pattern in their development, whether domestic or international, we must, as well, utilize the ability which Trans-Canada Air Lines has already demonstrated and seek standards of operation which through their uniformity will improve economic efficiency. It is, in consequence, obvious that any new companies established should be 'subsidiaries of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
To achieve these objectives the bill proposes that the governor in council may establish new corporations for the operation of air services, at the same time determining the capital of such corporations and naming the provisional directors, and that the shares of any corporation so established shall be offered for subscription to Trans-Canada Air Lines. The bill also empowers Trans-Canada Air ,Lines to acquire and dispose of shares in companies established to operate air services. In order to protect the position of any companies incorporated under this Act, and insure that they may always remain under government control, it is also provided that Trans-Canada Air Lines must always retain fifty-one per cent of the shares of any such company. As a matter of fact it is the present intention of the government that Trans-Canada Air Lines should be the complete and sole owner of any such corporations established for the operation of Canadian international air services and the provision I have just mentioned is merely intended to add flexibility to meet unforeseen circumstances.
Any new company established under the Act would in general have the powers that Trans-Canada Air Lines at present possesses. In respect of authorization for its operations it would be treated in the same fashion as Trans-Canada Air Lines; that is, the governor in council would in the-first instance designate the air services which the new company is to operate and would then authorize the minister responsible for civil aviation to enter into a contract with the. new corporation for the operation of these services. Arrangements for carriage of mail by any new company in-

Trans-Canada Air Lines
corporated under the act would be made directly with the Postmaster General on the authorization of the governor in council.
It is impossible at this point to describe the detailed plans for each of the three main international services I have outlined. The company or companies that may be required, the amount of capital involved, the nature of the contract that may be entered into, the exact route to be followed, the frequency of services, the traffic stops to be made and the rates to be charged are all matters which are under study, by the responsible agencies of the government, and which are subject to continu-_ ing negotiation with other governments. All I can say at the moment, is that of the three routes I have mentioned, first priority will be given to the north Atlantic air service, an operation which we hope will be ready in the relatively near future, second priority will be given to the service to the West Indies and latin America, althought it may well be a year or so before this service is in operation; while third priority will be given to the Pacific service, the establishment of which depends in time upon the clearing of the Pacific and the working out of cooperative arrangements there. We had earlier considered that the war against Japan might well involve a substantial delay before operations could be initiated, but recent victory has, of course, changed the picture so that it is now possible to plan in terms of a Pacific operation which we hope may be started almost as soon as our service to latin America.
The added powers which have been given to Trans-Canada Air Lines in respect of purchase and disposition of shares in other companies have been extended to cover not only subsidiaries set up under this act but to cover other companies operating air services. This provision is designed to improve the economic efficiency of our international operations for it is likely to prove to our advantage to make specific agreements with other air companies in countries served by the lines which we operate, so that these other companies may feed traffic into the Canadian services. Achievement of this objective may in turn require investment in, or assistance to, these other companies.
Similar considerations have governed the provision in the bill that empowers Trans-Canada Air'Lines to loan money to any new company incorporated as a subsidiary of Trans-Canada Air Lines. This will, for example, make it possible for the revenue from paying services to be used>, if necessary, as loans to assist in the establishment of new services as required. In short, to repeat what I have already stressed, the main intent of the bill is
to seek parliamentary approval for a satisfactory framework which will protect the interest of the people of Canada in respect of development of our air service; and at the same time make it possible for Trans-Canada Air Lines, subject to the approval of the minister and the governor in council to pursue a flexible policy designed to meet the varying conditions and contingencies that are likely to arise in the development of air transport, and to make the best possible arrangements to achieve economic efficiency on each route.
A further change proposed by the bill relates ' to the carriage of mail within Canada. Originally the statute establishing Trans-Canada Air Lines provided that payments by the post office for the carriage of mail within Canada should be on a sliding scale calculated annually on the basis of the revenue and costs of operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines during the preceding year. This was a formula designed at the time to satisfy the position on the main transcontinental service when it was reasonably certain that the number of schedules to be operated would be limited and that mail would be. initially the most substantial factor in the traffic carried. The growth of services within Canada and the modification of schedules on existing routes have changed this position substantially. Carriage of mail will always be of fundamental importance to air services, but other types of traffic have grown and are growing rapidly. Moreover, initiation of numerous new services and new' schedules means that conditions relative to carriage of mail vary from route to route. It has, therefore, become evident that more flexible pro- , visions are required in respect of payment for air mail carriage. Accordingly it is proposed that the governor in council be granted authority to repeal section 17 of the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act which provides the formula for mail payments, leaving merely the provision that the Postmaster General on authorization of the governor in council may enter into a contract with Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is our intention that when a new contract has been agreed upon, to govern payment for carriage of mail, the governor in council will take action to repeal section 17.
Finally, in accordance with the need for flexibility which I have already mentioned, it is provided in the bill that any contract which may be entered into w'ith Trans-Canada Air Lines by the minister responsible for civil aviation or by the postmaster general may be altered or amended from time to time as circumstances require on the authorization of the governor in council. Here again the reason for action is the fact that the development of civil aviation is taking place so
Trans-Canada Air Lines

rapidly that a long term contract such as was originally planned in the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act may well become out of date in certain respects. Before its ten-year period has elapsed that provision should be made for modification in accordance with rapidly-changing circumstances.
I believe it would be of assistance to members of this house in considering the bill if in closing I reviewed briefly the history and what I believe are the accomplishments of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
As I have indicated, Trans-Canada Air Lines was incorporated by act of parliament in 1937. Its task was to provide the swiftest possible system of transportation between communities scattered across a territory of
3,000	miles and thereby to more closely integrate the nation.
Prior to this legislation there had been an abundance of aviation activity within Canada, but nothing of a transcontinental design. Operations were, for the most part, of the "bush" variety, serving mining camps and isolated settlements. Numerous small companies, flying a great diversity of equipment on a "charter" or "contract" basis, moved large quantities of men and supplies. Some scheduled operations were in existence on the Pacific coast, into the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and along the north shore of the St. Lawrence and into the maritimes- but the country had no coordinated air transport. The railways remained the only east-west arteries of Canadian transcontinental transportation. By 1937 it had become 'evident that something more was needed; that a nation so vast in its distances and so various in its economic divisions could not afford to do without the. fullest advantages of time and distance-destroying aviation. So Trans-Canada Air Lines was designed to meet a great Canadian need.
How well has this organization met the responsibilities that were entrusted to it?
To begin with, it must be realized that in 1937 the airline began with nothing. The airport, meteorological and communication needed *to support scheduled services by large aircraft were almost non-existent. Much of the terrain through which the transcontinental route must be threaded was wilderness. Canadian experience with aviation of this type and on the scale intended was very limited.
Yet to-day,' just eight years later, Trans-Canada Air Lines is recognized as one of the world's foremost air transport organizations. Its aircraft move with precision between Sydney, Halifax, Moncton, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, London, Windsor, North Bay, Winnipeg, Regina, Lethbridge, Calgary, Edmon-

ton, Vancouver and Victoria. They also cross the border to New Work and fly daily to Newfoundland. Through the joint efforts of T.C.A. and the Canadian government, an elaborate airport and airways system has been evolved and a 'stout foundation is in readiness for the greater aeronautical development that is certain to come. T.C.A.'s operational standards and achievement are respected through the air transport industry. All this has been accomplished in a few short years.
Yet the true significance of T.C.A. is not to be found in any record of mere growth, but in the contribution that the still-young airline has made to Canada's well-being.
This country is one of vast distances and varied interests, relying for its coherence as a nation upon the development of wide loyalties and general understandings. The success of confederation has depended upon the slow growth of tolerances and the gradual destruction of sectionalism. In large measure, the basic problem has been a geographical one-how to bring into closer association the far-flung economic and racial entities that together comprise Canada-how to establish a real community of interests and responsibilities among a people scattered widely between two oceans.
Facilities for transportation and communication have been among our most powerful tools in the fashioning of 'Canadian unity. Without the railroads, Canada as we know it could never have evolved. The same is true of radio and telephone, of bus and of private automobile. All these have fostered an exchange of goods and ideas that to-day bear fruit in an ever-tightening economic and .political union.
T.C.A. serves in the same high tradition. For the past eight years it has brought the unprecedented speeds of modern aviation to bear upon the problems of Canada's geographical immensity and internal diversity; and so effective has been its work that Canadian distances have, already lost much of their old significance. To-day, the travelling Canadian with limited time at his disposal is not confined within a narrow radius of his own home. The entire nation lies just beyond the nearest airport and a new sense of nationhood is being fostered by Canada's new accessibility to its citizens. In particular, Canadian industry and business have received a major stimulus from air transport. The busy entrepreneur, salesman or technician can now fashion his activities and his ambitions on a national scale, secure in the knowledge that Canada is no longer days, but only twelve hours wide, and that time of travel has ceased to be a major

Trans-Canada Air Lines
obstacle to tihe development of broad markets, the surveys of distant territories and the supervision of wide-spread field organizations.
T.C.A.'s carriage of air mail between the developed communities of Canada has likewise contributed to a mounting national consciousness, by accelerating the written exchange of information and ideas to an extent difficult to over-estimate. More and more goods of perishable or urgent nature are moving by air and new domestic markets are opening for many a Canadian producer. T.C.A., the transcontinental airline, is quickening the tempo of our whole national life.	[DOT]
It has not been possible for some time to purchase the additional aircraft required for the full satisfaction of Canada's mainline* air transport needs. But, through the efficient use of existing equipment, T.C.A. has been able, since 1940 to triple its carriage of passengers, multiply by four its volume of air mail, by eight the weight of air express. Miles flown in 1944 exceed ten million.
In spite of the restrictive conditions of recent years, it is safe to claim that no other airline in the world has grown to such stature in so short a time. Moreover, the work has been done with efficiency and imagination and without waste. T.C.A.'s maintenance, dispatch and pilot technique and standards are famous; this aviation service that has grown into so powerful a sinew of our domestic strength has shown an eight year not revenue for its shareholders-the people of Canada.
It should be borne in mind that T.C.A. has functioned almost from itis beginning in a wartime economy. The airline was just two year's old when Germany marched on Poland. After that day it dedicated itself to the paramount task of speeding the final victory. No evaluation of T.C.A.'s national service is complete without mention of its war records.
