speakerposition: topic
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the conduct of this discussion so far has, to my mind, been eminently unsatisfactory. Three weeks ago, late at night, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services began his statement, which he was not able to complete. Some days later he was followed by the Minister of National Defence for Air, who made a statement on which there was some discussion. Some days later again, in the last ten minutes of an evening session, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services succeeded in completing his statement. Then, when the committee returned to this subject again, the same minister, speaking on behalf of the army, made a statement and one observation was offered afterward on the part of the opposition. I do not consider that this gives us a proper opportunity for that detailed and considered discussion which this matter warrants.
The minister's statement, dealing with past, present and future, is to be found in Hansard of October 2 and October 9. So far as the future is concerned, I do not quarrel with the attitude taken by the government when it considers that the international situation is such that it is hardly feasible to proclaim a definite permanent policy for the navy. Demobilization is still being carried on, and there are various reasons entering into the question of what Canada's navy in the future shall be which scarcely lend themselves to definite decision' at this time.
The minister deals with the past by doing little more than to bring up to date statements which have been made on previous occasions with regard to naval affairs. I take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of the services of men in the little ships. As the minister has said, a considerable portion of the work falling to the Royal Canadian Navy has been in connection with north Atlantic convoy duty. That is true, but mucn

Demobilization-Naval Services
service was given elsewhere as well: in the Mediterranean, off the coast of France, and particularly up and down the inhospitable coast on the eastern shores of this country.
Those little ships carried on their lonely vigils, ever looking out for evidence of enemy action, passing that information back to headquarters, where the positions of U-boats, either singly or in nests, could be plotted and charted, thus enabling those who directed the convoy system to devise the routes the convoys should take. They carried on that work in fog and in storms, facing the perils of the elements as -well as those of the enemy, and under such freezing conditions that the helms on these little vessels had to be used cautiously, lest the tons of ice in their top hampers rendered them top heavy.
We, whose lands have not been devastated in the least, as have the lands of our allies, are a little inclined to accept these services with all too little appreciation. Lives were lost, health was impaired, nerves were strained, and those men are coming back to take their part once more in civilian occupations. It will be wise of us indeed if, in dealing with such men, we allow sympathy to play its proper part. The practice of using convoys started very early in the war. At that time on both sides of the Atlantic there were only a few small vessels suitable for the work of guarding those convoys. They were hastily collected, hastily manned, and hastily gunned. They were used with the stiffening of iestroyers, the services of which were badly aeeded in other directions. This condition prevailed while corvettes were being designed and built. Those designs were improved, and the second editions were released. Frigates were built, until at last we were in a position to give adequate provision to the convoys of the north Atlantic.
Before the U-boat menace was overcome the command of the north Atlantic convoy passed into the hands of the Canadian navy, with headquarters at Halifax. The minister did well the other day in extolling the services rendered to us and to the allied nations by Rear Admiral L. M. Murray, who was in charge of the convoy system.
The minister referred to the fact that early in this year the Canadian navy had reached the peak of its strength, namely, 95,000. Demobilization has already disposed and is disposing of about half that number. He anticipates that by March the figure will have been reduced to some 10,000. He has pointed out that the actual strength of the permanent force of the navy is 534 officers and 3383 ratings, making a total of just under 4,000. 
So that to have the 10,000 by March he will have to obtain the services of some 6,000. With this in mind he has put forward a recruiting campaign, from which he expects to obtain new enlistments to sign on for four years service.
He will obtain the assistance of some in the navy who will express a willingness to serve for another two years in what we may call an interim force; and perhaps it would be more easily understood if we called it a temporary permanent force. Then he will have the cadets who will graduate from year to year from the Royal Canadian naval college.
I would ask the minister to give a detailed progress report of the recruiting scheme,, setting out when it started and how it has progressed. We read some weeks ago in the press something to the effect that- seventy per cent of those coming forward were new enlistments. but that those who were expressing their willingness to continue for two years and who are already in the service, were coming along in greater numbers. I would ask the minister in his progress report to. deal with the proportion which will be allowed between newly enlisted men and those who are desirous of continuing to serve. I would ask him also to describe the terms of service being offered these men.
For instance, are war-time pay and allowance rates to be carried on?	Is marriage
allowance to be continued? What sort of plan is in contemplation to take care of the length of time required for service pension? And, although this may not be a closely related subject, I would ask him to explain the position of those in the permanent force, and those who have been serving but who came in through the reserves. What will their position be with regard to war service gratuities? I understand that no further gratuities will accrue after next March.
What is the position of the man in the service to-day who, through his length of service, has earned a certain amount in war service gratuities? When will he receive those amounts, and in what form? The minister has referred to the joining up of the two forms of reserve into one reserve, for the future. Will he explain whether the reserve of the future will be comparable in terms of service with the reserves of the past. It seems to me that we must accept the fact that a reserve of that sort, the volunteer reserve of the past, the non-permanent active militia of the past, was a body of civilians who gave of their spare time to training and exercises in the establishments across Canada and who were

Demobilization-Naval Services
ready in times of annual leave or annual holidays to give of their time to service afloat. In that regard a good deal of assistance was given in the past by employers who facilitated leaves so that they would fit in with cruises. It does not seem to me that it is likely the minister can rely on members of the reserve to make up ships' companies of vessels to be retained in commission.
The minister also made reference to the sea cadet corps. I think his predecessor was the first Minister of National Defence to recognize and commend this corps. He expressed the opinion that we should look upon the sea cadet movement as being a fruitful source of sailors of the future. It was not started for that purpose; it was started more -with the idea of endeavouring to inculcate into the youth of Canada the principles of the Royal Navy and what that navy stood for as adopted on our behalf for the Royal Canadian Navy. It was to that end that the corps was carried on.
Two or three years ago the regulations governing the corps were amplified and brought up to date. To-day the sea cadet movement in Canada is recognized as being a far more efficient body than it was before. I trust the time is not far distant when the government will be able to give a little more assistance to the sea cadet corps. I have been interested in this movement for a good many years. There are two small corps in my immediate neighbourhood, one at Kelowna and one at Penticton. I know full well, particularly in the years of depression, the grave difficulty we had to keep those corps going. They were located in rural areas where there was no large city population to appeal to, and those of us who were particularly interested in the movement had to dig down into our pockets to keep them going.
Then the. war came along and the numbers increased considerably. Just a day or two ago 1 received a letter from the president of the sea cadet corps "Grenville" in Kelowna, of which I should like to read three sentences. He is making his annual appeal to the public of that neighbourhood for financial support for the corps, and he says;
From its ranks, thirty boys are now serving in the navy, seven in the mercantile marine, eighteen in the army, and twenty in the air force.	.
Seven have been killed in action, three decorated and .one mentioned in dispatches.
The training these boys have received has served in good stead during the crisis of war. but should be continued with equal vigour during the peace, in inculcating discipline, ability of leadership, character building, and willingness to seTve.
I agree entirely with the statement made by the president of that organization. I would emphasize the fact that he. is referring to a small body that has carried on for about a dozen years. There are many in that neighbourhood who deeply appreciate what these boys have been taught.
About half-way through his statement the minister said that he would turn from men to ships. I wish that he, having turned to ships, had given the committee some more detailed information with regard to ships. At the present time we are without knowledge as to what ships are to serve on either of the coasts of Canada. A little light was thrown on this subject by the minister's predecessor who on one occasion said that a total strength of
9.000	was being considered. He then made a statement which to my mind was a strange statement for a minister to make of his own department. He said that he considered that figure too small and hoped it would be increased to 15,000. The minister put it at 10,000.
A little light was thrown on the subject, again in what I think was a most unusual way. At a press interview the senior officer on the Pacific coast stated that Canada's postwar navy would be much larger than her prewar navy and that it would consist of cruisers, fleet aeroplane carriers, destroyers and frigates, which would be in equal numbers on either coast. I do not know whether the minister authorized that statement to be made or approved its having been made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I contend that this is the place where we should be given that information. The proper place to give that information surely is in the statement which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has made to this house. In referring to ships he referred to the cruiser Uganda, which was recently brought back to the Pacific coast in order to dispense with the services of those on board who desired demobilization. He has not told us whether her complement has again been filled up, or what her purpose will foe now.
He has referred to the cruiser Ontario now serving with the Royal Navy in the Pacific. We want 'to know whether she is to be brought back shortly for a similar purpose, how rapidly her complement will be restored and what she will then be used for. Two days ago the antiaircraft cruiser Prince Robert docked at Esqui-malt, having brought home released prisoners of war from the Pacific. I presume that the same process will go on in connection with the Prince Robert and that those of the ship's company who desire to be demobilized will be

Demobilization^-Naval Services
dispensed with. Are we to understand that her complement will then be brought up again? What will she be used for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
She is to be declared
Burplus.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is one of the pieces of information with regard to our ships that I should have thought the minister would make in his statement. He then referred to the four Tribals built in Canada, one in commission, two to be commissioned next year and the fourth to be commissioned in 1947. The Tribals are admirable ships, but they are not quite as admirable as they were some six or seven years ago when the Royal Navy introduced them. They are far from being obsolete now, but they are moving along the road to obsolescence. Ahead of them on that road are the River class, and still further ahead on that road to obsolescence are those older destroyers upon which we presumably placed some reliance. The minister simply referred to the Tribals and then stopped. He made no reference to the Crescent class. When we first heard of the class known as the Crescent, we knew that they were the last word in destroyers, and that Canada was to have four of them. We know that one is commissioned and already on her way to the Pacific coast. We believe that the second will be commissioned in the course of the next few weeks, and we know nothing of the third and the fourth. Will the minister make a statement informing us of the position with regard to the Crescents? The Crescents are so far ahead of the Tribals because they have been outfitted with all these various discoveries of the war. The armament is different; the scientific instruments are different; the electrical installations are brought up to date. They are, I suppose, the last word in destroyers to-day. We were to have four, and we believe that we know something about two.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
At six o'clock I was
drawing attention to the very considerable amount of additional information that we look to the minister to provide us with so that we may get a far more complete picture of the Canadian navy to-day and of the immediate future. He has made no reference whatever to

the naval air service; yet that subj ect was drawn to our attention, when the minister for air was before the committee, by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who expressed his opinion, and his opinion must carry considerable weight with us because of the excellence of the service which he rendered to us and to the allied nations when he was minister for air. He expressed an opinion which would not of necessity be agreed to by the minister for naval services, and certainly we look to this occasion for a statement of the government's views with regard to the immediate future of the naval air service. We want him to tell us how many pilots we have, the number of aircrew, aircraftmen serving in the ships and the aircraft at our disposal, and to what extent those figures which he will give us may be expanded.
I wish now to attempt an analysis of the ships which are at our disposal, and of the men to man them. We get very little help from the minister's statement in that regard. There is a short paragraph near the end of his statement which reads:
It is now proposed that at the outset Canada's peace-time navy should comprise two cruisers, probably two light fleet carriers, ten to twelve destroyers and the necessary ancillary craft, all of these of the latest and most ' modern type, while in reserve and for training purposes we will continue to hold a certain number of frigates. Such an establishment will require a force of about ten thousand officers and men.
There is a rule of thumb, which has obtained in naval circles for a great number of years, that for each man afloat there should be a man ashore. There would be men undergoing initial training, and their instructors; those carrying out technical courses with a view to promotion, and their instructors; the establishment on both coasts, with the necessary employees; headquarters here in Ottawa with its various branches, with pay and personnel; ordnance technical branches, each with its director and those serving under him.
It is interesting to note that the rule of thumb appears to apply with some accuracy to the very small figures of Canada's pre-war navy. At that time there were five ships afloat. There were destroyers. They were smaller than Tribal and their complement was probably something under two hundred. Shall we say that 900 were afloat in those two ships? Double that figure and you have just about the strength of Canada's pre-war navy. If we apply it to these ten thousand we find ourselves with 5,000-afloat and if those 5,000 are disposed in ships which are serving on each coast, and they are of equal size, we have 2,500 men afloat on either coast.

Demobilization-Naval Services
The complement of one of our cruisers is from 800 to 900, and on the small aircraft carrier, from 1,000 to 1500, so that we find that the best part of 2,000 of the 2,500 on either coast is taken up in the cruiser and the aircraft carrier. The complement of a Tribal is 220 to 240, so that if there be one Tribal attached on either coast we have used up 2,220 or so of the 2,500 and we have, say, 280 to dispose of.
One of the mistakes we made in the prewar navy was that we did not have in service auxiliary vessels. In peace time some of the duties of the Canadian navy on either coast consist of such work as training, and support of the Department of Justice and the Department of National Revenue in their requirements. and such work would be far better carried out by auxiliary vessels than by the far more expensive vessels such as destroyers.
We arrive, then, at one cruiser, one small aircraft carrier and one Tribal, and if we choose to add a second Tribal there is then very little left in the way of man-power for any ancillary vessels at all. I suggest that a squadron composed of one cruiser, one aircraft carrier, one destroyer and perhaps some, ancillary vessels is a most unhandy squadron to do anything with. If the two were added together they would be an equally unhandy fleet unit. In the plans which have been laid down for us in the past, hon. members will remember that after the great war Lord Jellicoe paid a visit to the dominions and expressed his opinion, based on his long experience, as to what the dominion navies might see fit. to be made up of. I do not think his report was ever adopted as the building programme in Canada, but it carried weight and it was of interest.
I do not propose to recount what it was composed of, but it did consist of a squadron on either coast. Also, in years since that, our naval staff has on more than one occasion prepared building programmes, and with the experience which our naval staff has had we may be quite sure they were looking upon it as minimum strength for which they were providing. They also required that there should be a service on either coast.
What are the duties of the Canadian navy in war time? Offence, defence, the capability of joining together in one fleet unit for war operations; and in peace also to join together for exercises, preferably fleet exercises, with the fleet of the Royal Navy. These exercises have all too seldom been held in the past. The idea has always been that they should be there prepared to carry out exercises, and the duties which fell to their lot, so that they might be joined together, if it were required,
to act as a fleet unit. In peace time, what is the duty of a squadron on either coast, besides actual defence of our neutrality? It has been to carry out certain necessary work of the departments on the coast, to carry out training and to protect and police those lanes on which our commerce crosses the seas, and particularly in those focal areas near our coasts north and south of Vancouver island, north and south of Newfoundland, around the coasts of Nova Scotia to the bay of Fundy, all for the purpose of showing to the world that we have naval vessels afloat. If we do that there is the least likelihood that lawlessness will raise its head on the high seas.
I look to the minister for a great deal more information than he has yet given us. I would conclude my remarks with this suggestion, that it is entirely wrong for us to extol the magnificence of Canada's commerce, to boast that we are the fourth trading nation in the world and at the same time to provide inadequate naval defence for that commerce in the focal areas. We must be ready. All too often m the past, in naval discussions which have had to do with the size and disposition of Canada's navy, we have come across such a remark as this: "The force should be sufficient ufitil support arrives." I ask, from where will that support come? It surely must come, and can only come, from the navies of other countries, navies built and maintained by the taxpayers of another country, not from our pockets. It seems to me that we do not save our face when we extol the magnificence of our commerce if we are not prepared to do our share in defending it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Yale has made a number of points which I shall endeavour to answer. First, let me say that on one I am in complete agreement with him. I, too, am far from satisfied with the arrangements as they have developed for presenting the defence estimates. I have been spending a good deal of time in sitting here waiting to get to my estimates, but all to no purpose. No one is entirely to blame for that situation. It has been due in part at least to getting certain matters through, namely, the united nations agreement, the food agreement, and so on. I may say also that the fault is not entirely due to the government. There has been a certain amount of discussion taking place on the other side. But now that we have finally' reached them, and I hope that with a reasonable degree of luck we shall be able to get through them promptly.
The hon. member first asked me to give him some information as to the recruiting campaign for the interim force. Let me say at once that
Demobilization-Naval Services

there has been no recruiting campaign at all. A month or six weeks ago we announced the basis on which men would be taken in the interim force in the three services, pending determination as to the terms and conditions on which our permanent forces will be set up. We realized at that time that that was not a very satisfactory basis on which to appeal to a man to stay in the army, but we did want to indicate to those who were in process of being demobilized at that time that we needed the young men who had gained experience in this war in our permanent forces, and that we hoped that some of them (would consider staying on. The committee will recall that when making that statement with respect to the army last week I was able to indicate a little more definitely the terms, and conditions which *would apply to the permanent forces in all three services, and now we are able to give a little better idea as to what the size of those forces will be. I was unable to say exactly what the scale of pay and allowances would be, but a committee has been set up. It is working on the matter now with a view to arriving at a pay scale which will be reasonably uniform between the three services. As I said in my statement, the pay will be good pay. We have not any intention of setting up a cheap permanent force. We have given an undertaking to men when they sign up now in the interim forces that a definite statement will be made not later than March 31 next.
I myself hope that I shall be in a position to make it much earlier, but that is the final deadline we have set. We have said to those men who may decide now to sign up in the interim forces: "If you do not wish to stay on in the permanent forces when you know what the terms and conditions are to be we will relieve you of your undertaking to serve until September 30, 1947." This is not a complete answer to them, but all the man is taking a chance on-if I may put it in that way-is that he is .saying: "Although I am entitled to be demobilized now.I will not go out until the terms and conditions are finally announced which will not be later than next March, and then I can decide whether or not I want to stay in." The only chance he is taking is that he may lose an attractive employment opportunity in the meantime.
We have announced that service in this war, and in the interim forces, will avail as service for purposes of pension. I am informed that that is a point which is of some considerable importance to men who are contemplating joining the services. Again an interdepartmental committee has been working on the question of a pension plan. Its work is well advanced and we shall be in a position to announce that plan at the latest by March 31.



[DOT]3
The committee will recall that the other conditions I mentioned were that promotion will be available to junior officers on the basis of merit even in peace time, and the other conditions which I outlined. Therefore I think that those who may be interested in making the services a career have some fair indication now as to what the conditions are likely to be. It is true they will not know definitely until March 31 at the latest, but I hope that the committee will be 'able to complete its work as to pay scales and one thing and another before that date. At the moment the chief basic task which is occupying the attention of our three services-I know it is the case in the navy and army and I am sure it is the case in the service over which my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air, presides -is the demobilization programme. This is taking the attention of a very large proportion of our staff. In both the navy-and I am talking about the navy now-and the army we do not contemplate putting on what one might describe as a recruiting campaign until early in the year. I am not sure myself whether that may not be a bit too early, because, if I remember my own experience, the psychology now is that there is a desire to get out. Until we get a little farther advanced along that road I do not know that a good many chaps who may now want to make the service a career are yet prepared to make a definite decision. In any event, speaking now for the navy, I may say it is not our intention to attempt to put on any organized recruiting campaign, if I may so describe it, until early in the year.

Have any come forward
so far?	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes. We are not so badly off as far as officers are concerned; we could do with more ratings. I have been personally more concerned in seeing that some of the younger officers with combat experience in this war and good technical qualifications may be induced now to make the service a career before they have left and gone out and established themselves in civil life. It was for that reason that we have been endeavouring to give as definite an indication as we could of the conditions under which they would be serving in a peace-time force.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to give figures?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am not at the moment; I could give them a little later when we are discussing the naval estimates. I have not them before me at the moment. They are appre-

Demobilization-Naval Services
ciable, but they are not large. Frankly, that is not a matter which at the moment is giving us any particular concern. I am speaking of the navy now. We have been concentrating on getting certain key officers, or trying to get them. I am advised by the staff there is no such pessimism. At the appropriate time they will be able to get all the men they need for the post-war navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about the technical men?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is always a problem. Those are the men on whom they are concentrating now; but after all, the Japanese war only ended less than two .months ago, and although our demobilization has been proceeding pretty rapidly we still have a fairly substantial number of men in the navy. I feel reasonably sure that even a number of those who have taken their discharge will come back a little later and ask to be allowed to take on the navy again as a career. Basing my statement on the advice I have had from my officers, I do not really anticipate there will be any serious difficulty in getting the right type of men, the type we want, for our post-war navy. We want to get as many as possible of the younger men, including the younger technical men such as those to whom my hon. friend has referred.
The next point the hon. member for Yale raised was the matter of reserves. I say to him at once that we have not yet completed our definite plans as to the organization of our new reserve set-up. The staff are now working on a submission for an appropriate order in council setting out the terms and conditions of that reserve. I anticipate it will be available very shortly, certainly well within the time we shall need to have it available; but as I indicated a moment ago, at the moment the priority as far as the ' planners and the staff are concerned is to see that the demobilization machine operates smoothly. At the same time we are working on the plans for the reserve, but I am not yet in a position to make any definite public statement as to just what those terms and conditions will be.
The hon. member referred to the value of the sea cadet movement. I am glad he did so, because personally I feel that this movement is performing a most valuable role in our naval set-up. We have never considered that we were a seafaring nation, but during this war we have shown that lads can come from the central provinces and make fine sailors. One way to develop that spirit is,
I think by having these sea cadets corps scattered about in the interior of Canada, 47696-87
where these young lads can learn something about seafaring matters. If I might speak personally, I can say that one of my own boys has found it extremely interesting, and he never had anything to do with seafaring matters until he joined the corps.
Then my hon. friend asked as to the disposition of ships as between the two coasts. I am not in a position nor do I propose to make any definite statement as to the exact disposition of our available ships between the east coast and the west coast. I will say this, however, that Canada is a two-coast country and certainly we have to operate a two-coast navy. Our navy is not to be concentrated on either one or the other coast. If the members of the committee will look at the mathematical total of our ships they will see that by and large the figures I have given can be readily divided by two. I am not prepared to say that we shall have one cruiser on the east coast and one on the west coast at all times, or that we shall have one carrier on the east coast and one on the west coast at all times, and the same with the destroyers. I will say that there will be a substantial portion of our fleet units operating on each of the two coasts.
My hon. friend asked some questions about the cruiser Uganda. As the committee knows, the Uganda returned to Esquimalt some time ago, just before the end of the Japanese war, in order to enable those of her personnel who had not volunteered for Pacific duty to be replaced. She is still at Esquimalt. Two or three days ago we had word from Admiral Fraser, commander of the British Pacific fleet, that the Ontario was no longer required with that fleet. I am pleased to be able to tell the committee that she is now starting on her way back to Canada and I anticipate will arrive within the next month, certainly well before Christmas. The Prince Robert has already arrived at Esquimalt, and as I indicated in an interjection to my hon. friend's remarks this afternoon, we no longer have need for her so that she will be declared surplus and disposed of in the ordinary way. As some of the committee may not know, she was a merchant ship converted to an antiaircraft cruiser for operations in the Pacific. That type of ship is no longer required, so that we do not contemplate retaining her and she will be disposed of.
Now a word as to destroyers. It is true that in my preliminary statement to the committee I did not indicate perhaps as definitely as I might have, or as I am quite 'willing to, what destroyers we would be having in our initial post-war fleet; but as my hon.

Demobilization-Naval Services

friend knows, and as he indicated this afternoon, we now have the four Tribals in operation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Four Tribals in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, four in operation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: In his statement the minister said that two would be commissioned in 1946 and one in 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Those are the ones being constructed. We have four Tribals now in operation and the three now being constructed. As I indicated in my statement, the final one will be completed in 1947. We have two of the V-class fleet destroyers; we have two Crescents, one of which is in Kingston Jamaica, to-day and on her way to the west coast, while the other, as my hon. friend indicated, will be commissioned very shortly. We also have at present one old River-class destroyer which for the moment we contemplate using for training purposes. I am not competent to say whether the Tribals are more modern or more effective than the Crescents. I had never heard that the Crescent was more efficient or more effective than the Tribal. The Crescent is a later type destroyer, it is true, but the Tribal is the largest destroyer in any modern fleet. As its armament it has eight guns and four tubes as against four guns and four tubes for the Crescent, and the vice chief of the naval staff, who had personal experience in operating the Haida, one of these ships in the channel, tells me he found the extra fire power of the Tribal a pretty satisfactory thing to have. In any event no one can say with certainty that the Crescent is a more effective, more efficient or more satisfactory destroyer to have than the Tribal. It is true that the Crescent, as now coming out of the yards, has a more modern type of radar gun control equipment, but that equipment can and will be installed in the Tribals. So that I am not competent to argue with anybody as to the relative merits of design as between the Tribal and the Crescent, but I can say with certainty that both are up-to-date, modern destroyers, and I think the Tribals we have now, with the additional ones we expect to have, should prove very satisfactory units for the Canadian naval service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What about the other two Crescent destroyers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As my hon, friend knows, those Crescents are on loan, and at the moment we do not propose to expand the number of our destroyers. The total number, as my hon. friend will remember, is four

Tribals in operation and three under construction; two V-class fleet destroyers, which are modern destroyers, and two Crescents, making up the ten destroyers to which I referred in my statement. If more are needed they can be added at any time. However, at the outset those units to which I referred in my statement, the two cruisers, two light fleet carriers, and ten destroyers, with the usual auxiliary craft such as frigates and minesweepers in reserve, I think constitute a good, workable little fleet to start with. It can be easily expanded if needs be, but that is the fleet which the government and staff feel is a satisfactory, workable type of fleet with which to start our peace-time navy and, as plans at present exist, that is the basis on which we intend to proceed.
As to the naval air service, as the committee knows plans prior to the termination of the Pacific war contemplated our manning two lijght fleet carriers' for Pacific operations. Those carriers were to be on loan from the Royal Navy. They are now being constructed in British yards. The first will be commissioned about January 15 and, according to present information, the other will not be completed until about six or seven months later.
We had arranged for the necessary flying personnel from Canadians who were serving in the fleet air arm with the Royal Navy and for other Canadians who were taken indirectly into the R.C.N.V.R. as flymg personnel and trained, of course, in the fleet air arm, to man those two carriers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How many aircraft would each ship carry?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I cannot answer that at the moment, but I can get the information quickly, and I shall give it later on. That flying personnel was, of course, "hostilities only" personnel. They were not men signing on for a permanent naval career. So that in respect of carriers as in respect of other units in tlie fleet it will now be necessary to provide the personnel from men who will sign on either as interim force or, better still, of course, in the permanent force.
My good friend the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) in the debate the other night-unfortunately I was not here

 raised the question, or possibly I should say made the suggestion, that careful consideration should be given to the advisability of establishing a separate fleet air arm. I read his. remarks carefully and I note that he did not say that he was definitely against it. He did say that he felt most careful and serious consideration should be given to the ad-

. Demobilization-Naval Services
visability of setting up such a separate fleet air arm because of the probable duplication of staff, and the like. No separate fleet air arm has yet been authorized, but it is contemplated. I think, after having given the matter a considerable amount of study myself, it is desirable that there should be a separate branch of the naval service including flying personnel who are naval officers. It is intended that these officers should be naval officers, as well as flying officers. In other words, they should be full-fledged executive officers, and after training as pilots and flying as pilots or observers on these carriers, in due course they should take their places as ordinary executive officers, let us say, as second in command, or as commander of a carrier. That is the practice which has been followed in other fleets, notably in the Royal Navy and in the United States navy and there is much to recommend it.
Such study as I have been able to give to the matter thus far indicates that there would not be any serious duplication of effort. I understand that discussions are now going on between the navy and the air force with a view to coordinating the training of pilots for fleet purposes. It is quite evident we shall have to maintain air establishments on both east and west coasts, and it would be very easy to arrange that those establishments should conduct training jointly for naval personnel and for those who may contemplate serving in the air force. Then the naval personnel, when they have had their preliminary training at land aerodromes, can get their further training on the two carriers. At any rate, that is the plan, as it has been worked out up to the present time, and it strikes me as being a fairly reasonable sort of plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does Canada now own any aircraft suitable for naval air service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, we do. We were able to obtain some. While I have not the figures, the fact is that the British were able to provide us with some aircraft they had at Dartmouth, which were flying on carriers in the Atlantic. Those aircraft are available to us now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: What are they?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I cannot remember just
now. but I can get the information.
The hon. member asked for more details as to how the estimated figures of 10,000 personnel are made up. I do not think I can do better than place on Hansard a summary of the number of officers and ratings 47696-87J
who, it is contemplated, would be serving afloat, and perhaps in total the number serving ashore. The following table will set out that information:

Then, for shore establishments, we have a total of 3,999 or almost 4,000, making an estimated grand total of 10,000. This, of course, contemplates that in the peace-time establishment there will be a considerable number of civilian employees. During the war in our shipyards and dockyards we had a great many men in naval uniforms, who were really not sailors. They were doing work such as plumbing, mechanical work and that sort of thing. But in peace time, in addition to the uniformed personnel there would of course be a considerable number of civilian personnel performing duties which during the war were performed by men in uniform.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: About how many?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have no definite estimate as to that. It is pretty hard to say just at the present time. However, I can indicate generally that there would be a considerable number.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Why the increase in
civil salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is one reason, of
course. During the demobilization period we are replacing uniformed personnel as rapidly as possible with civilian personnel. For instance, in a place like national defence headquarters at Ottawa, where we can get a civilian grade 1 clerk to do a Wren's work, we do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What is the complement of a tribal destroyer?
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I shall have to ask ray
hon. friend to let that question stand. The information will be available in a few moments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
In connection with the navy,
when a man signs on for the interim force how long is it before he knows whether or not he is accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I would say he knows at
once. If he signs on I would say he is accepted. If he applies to his commanding officer and says, "I would like to serve in the interim force," then that of course is subject to acceptance. The commanding officer may take some time to make his decision. If he signs on, he knows right then and there that he is in.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have been told that the maximum number of men in the navy was 95,000. Before we can intelligently discuss these estimates I think we should know how many men are in the service to-day and how many are being discharged' daily. We would then have some basis for checking up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: About'fifty-three per cent are out to date. I shall have the exact figure in a moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: How many are you letting out a day?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know that it follows an exact daily average. For the last month or two it has gone on at the rate of about 10,000 a month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Over 50,000 have been discharged from the navy up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: About fifty-three per cent of the total. I do not know that we have discharged' 53,000 to date. Those actually out .or on the way out up to October 31 number 46,773, or 53-2 per cent of the total.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What information is
given to recruits entering the interim service as to the instructions they will recieve or what educational facilities and privileges will be accorded to them during their term of service? They must sign on for two years or probably five years. I think a great number of the men who will volunteer for that period *would want to know what trades they can learn, so that when they return to civil life at the expiry of their# time in two or five years, as the case may be, they will have some equipment to undertake civilian life.
They will also want to know what reestablishment privileges they will have when their term has expired. Just now many forms of assistance are given to our armed forces which are not now available to the man who goes

into the interim force. I think the minister should give more particulars as to the possibilities that are open to these men, or what inducements are being offered for their going into the service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As I say, a man must make up his mind no later than March 31 whether he wants to stay in the interim force. As to pay, allowances and all the rest, they are exactly the same as he is now receiving. We are taking no new men into the interim force; it is open only to men who are now in the service or who have just been discharged, men who have had training and experience during the war. They will continue to receive the same pay and allowances and all the rest as they received during the war. They are entitled to gratuity,- the rehabilitation grant and reestablishment credits, as well as the various other benefits, educational and the like. I should have answered that question when replying to the hon. member for Yale when he asked what the situation would be with respect to gratuities, and so on.
This matter is now being discussed. It has not yet been settled as to when that will be paid. The rights will continue to accrue to not later than March 31 next, at which time the gratuities, reestablishment credits and so on will cease to accrue. It has not yet been decided whether the man who signs on for a year or two will be paid his gratuity now, but that is being discussed. There is some difference of view between the three services.
As to the man who goes into the permanent force for five years, I must confess that this is a matter which is entirely new to me. If he is now a member of the forces he retains his right to gratuity, reestablishment credits and so on. However, I am afraid I shall have to inquire as to where he would stand if he wanted to take a university education at the end of five years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
A man is not entitled to many of these benefits until he takes 'his discharge. Therefore, if he continues in the interim force or enters the permanent force, he would not take his discharge. Then a man may want to continue his education. I think these men should know what qualifications they can acquire by continuing in the interim or permanent force. The department should give consideration to setting up some sort of vocational training to be coordinated with the military or naval training that these men will receive. This would prove an inducement to the men because they would know they would not be totally helpless should they desire to ask for their discharge to enter civilian life again.

Demobilization-Naval Services
There is also the problem of housing for the wives and families of these men. Will they	be able	to take	advantage of government	loans	in	order to	establish their familiesin homes? I am sure that many hon. members	know	of	men in	the permanent armywho	have	wives and	children whom they
would like to get settled in homes of their own. I understand that at the present time they must have their discharge before they can take advantage of the Veterans Land Act. I understand that if a man is in the permanent force he must get a written statement from his commanding officer that he will remain in the community for approximately ten years.
I know of one or two cases that I want to have ironed out in some way. One man has served during the war and he would like to get established with his family. He would like to go into the permanent force rather than take his discharge, but if he does that he may be transferred to another community. The fact that a man joins the permanent force does not relieve him of responsibility to his wife and children, but it should not react to his disadvantage in connection with rehabilitation grants and other benefits.
I have another case that has just been drawn to my attention. This man was in the permanent force before serving overseas and he intends to remain in that force. He wants to buy in his parental neighbourhood a home in which to establish his wife and children, but he cannot get any benefits under the Veterans Land Act until he obtains his discharge. He may then rejoin the permanent force, but even then he must get a certificate from his commanding officer that he is likely to be kept in the community for the next ten years.
This makes it almost impossible for these men to take advantage of these provisions. I think these matters should be made clear to the men in the three forces because at present it is very disquieting to them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend has raised some very good points. A man joining the interim force or the permanent force does not lose any of the benefits to which he is entitled as a result of having served in the war. I will see that my hon. friend's remarks are brought to the attention of the staff who are now working on that very problem. As to giving assurances as to the type of vocational training that will be given men in the permanent navy during peace time, I am not in a position to say anything about that just now. If a man joins as a tradesman he is bound to get training as a mechanic or an
engineer, but I do not think I can give any assurance that definite vocational training courses will be established. I will bear my hon. friend's remarks in mind and discuss them with the staff.
While I am on my feet I may say that the complement of the Tribal destroyer in wartime is 275 men. With the reduction to about four-fifths of the wartime complement, the complement now will be 220 men. As to the aircraft on our light fleet carriers, there is one squadron of twelve bombers or Fireflies. Then we have one squadron of eighteen fighters, Seafires, making a total of thirty.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does the minister say that at the moment no new enlistments are being taken in?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No; what I said was that we are taking in no enlistments in the interim force. I think we are taking enlistments in the permanent force. A man with no previous naval training cannot join the interim force; he must join the permanent force.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The statement was made in the press a few weeks ago that 70 per cent of those coming forward were new enlistments who were signing on for a four-year period, and that the others coming in from the present service were coming in in greater numbers than they had been. Is that totally incorrect?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I have not heard of thdse percentages and I would be surprised if they were accurate. I will verify the percentages and give more definite information later. But I know that we are not taking large numbers into the permanent force. Up to comparatively recently we were not anxious to do so because we w-anted to get the scale of pay and allowances clarified, and with very large of wartime personnel still in the service we were not particularly anxious to take into the permanent service new men with no naval training.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
When the war estimates first came up for consideration we outlined to the committee four broad principles concerning our defence forces of the future which we asked everybody in the house to endorse. One of those principles was that we must not destroy the efficiency of any of our forces. All the Canadian forces have done splendid work. I think the time element in connection with enlistments for the permanent forces is very important, and just at this time the government must be very careful or they might destroy the efficiency of the forces for a long time to come. Take the navy. The
Demobilization-Naval Services

minister has admitted to-night that not very much attention is being paid to getting any recruits. For the moment they are not bothering very much about the navy of the future.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I said, new men with no naval training.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I can understand that. It is only natural that the department should be concerned primarily at the present time with demobilization, but I think they must put far more emphasis than they have been doing on the navy of the future. Otherwise they are apt to wake up next year and find that they cannot get the men, that they have these ships tied up at the docks on both coasts without men to man them. If that should happen it will be very difficult to build up an efficient navy again. I would urge upon the minister that he change his outlook a bit. He said this evening that the psychology now was to get out, that everybody wanted1 to get out of the navy. I think he is quite wrong there. I have had young men come to me and say that they were eager to make a career of the navy, but that they could not do so and would not feel justified in doing so until they had more of a lead from the government; more information as to what chance there would be of a successful career in the navy.
The very fact that the department have set a total of 10,000 personnel for the navy seems to me to indicate a failure to grasp the problem. We are told by the highest authorities n the country that 10,000 will not be sufficient ;o man the ships that have been listed by the minister to-night. That may or may not be mrrect. Of course, we are in the hands of the experts who understand these matters, but there is at least room for suspicion that this figure of 10,000 is not adequate to ensure that the ships we have or are getting will be properly manned. Does the minister not think it would be wise to raise his sights a little in order to be sure that we shall have enough men? Nobody wants to join a force that is going to be weak; to join a navy that is not going to be able to make the cruises that should be made by an efficient modern navy. I would ask the minister to check over with his officials that question of the numbers to be in the permanent navy just to make sure that 10,000 will be ample. We are very dubious about it, and if the minister starts off with too few I am afraid that it will be difficult to maintain an efficient navy. We are very much concerned lest any one of the forces be allowed to slip back in this interim period, and we would ask the government not to be too smug about having plenty of time to get the forces converted from a war-time to a peace-time basis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The question I wish to direct to the minister is one in which I think a great many Canadians are interested, namely, what use is being made of Canada's larger naval vesels in bringing back Canadian troops from the old country? I understand that the smaller vessels will not make efficient troop transports, but are there not some larger vessels that could bring perhaps 350 in one trip? What larger vessels have we that might be used in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
We really have no naval
vessels suited to the transport of troops across the Atlantic in winter. We have the auxiliary aircraft carrier Puncher, which has been and still is operating regularly transporting troops, carrying about 200 each trip. We have brought back a considerable number on the older class of destroyers, and a good many have been ferried from Newfoundland. But many of our destroyers have been operating steadily under difficult conditions for a number of years now, and they bady need refitting. In any event, a destroyer is not suited to carrying troops across the Atlantic particularly in winter; I would not want to be one of the troops on them; they are not designed or fitted to transport troops, and the staff tell me that they cannot be used for that purpose. The Puncher is being used and will continue to be used. As my hon. friend indicated, corvettes and frigates for very much the same reason are not suited for the transport of troops, so that unfortunately the naval craft we have are not of. the type suitable for transporting troops across the Atlantic, particularly in winter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
With regard to the
permanent force, how many have transferred from the present force to the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will take note of the question and try to give that information later.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I want to speak to the
question which has been raised by the hon. member for Yale and the hon. member for Vancouver South. I refer to the question of securing sufficient suitable personnel for the navy. My remarks will be applicable, of course, to all three services. I am apprehensive that the government's policy is not going to meet the case. Their own requirements are
55,000	men, and as I shall go on to suggest in the particular case of the navy, there are many people in this house and in the country who believe that figure should be larger. Fifty-five thousand for peace-time service is a very large figure at which to shoot in this country, and I think this whole problem has been approached by the miiiister, if he will not mind my using the word, in too casual an attitude. He has a very great responsibility on his

Demobilization-Naval Services
shoulders at the present time, and in the debate on these estimates I have not seen that he realizes how big that responsibility is.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Appearances are very deceptive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister says that appearances are very deceptive. That is perfectly true, but I say to him that if he gives the same impression to prospective recruits for his forces as he gives to me he will not get many recruits. I want, however, before I get on with too much criticism of his policy, to say one thing, and that is that the statement he made with regard to the terms of service, when he spoke on the army estimates, has done a great deal to clear up difficulties we have been having up to the present time in understanding his policy, and difficulties which prospective soldiers, sailors and airmen have been having in deciding whether to go into civil life or into the services. It was a very good statement and laid down good principles and it will do much to clear up doubts in the minds of those going into- the services. But that statement is not enough. I say that the whole policy the minister has put forward in regard to the naval services is one of indecision, indecision on size, indecision on principles, indecision on terms of service.
I wish to go over the whole question before I finish because I am going to suggest that there was no need whatever for any indecision in respect of any of these mattens. There are two essentials before you will have officers and men joining your services. The first essential is that the rates of pay, pension and working conditions shall be such as to attract young men. That is the part where the minister has put forward his best effort, but even that is not as complete as it could be or as it should be, although it goes quite a long way. The second essential, however, is the assurance of a continuing force sufficient to warrant, to a man who goes into the navy, a career. Men will not join the services just because the rates of pay are satisfactory if they do not know that those services will continue to exist in sufficient strength to give them a goal to shoot, at in life. That is what they want and it is not only good conditions of service which will bring them into the forces.
Both ministers for the defence services, in bringing down their estimates, have based their inability to make a statement, their desire to have an interim force, and their uncertainty about the future, upon the fact that they do not know what the obligations of the country will be under the united nations charter and also upon the fact that they do not know what the atomic bomb is going to do to the present types of service.
I realize that the matter is difficult to decide; I realize there is a problem there. But I do say this, and I want this to be clearly understood, that no one on this side asks the ministers for any rigidity in their policy. The last thing that we want in navy, army or air force is rigidity of numbers, rigidity of size, rigidity of weapons, rigidity of anything whatever. We must not have that rigidity. But it is possible to go too far the other way and to be too indefinite, and I say that the minister has been too indefinite and that our recruiting will suffer for it.
Let us take the second of the two essentials I gave, career and terms of service. I want to deal first of all with the question of career. What has the minister told us of the future navy? He has told us a little more to-night than we knew before, but still not very much. He has given us the size of the force in men and ships but has not laid down the policy or the principles which have governed the administration in arriving at these sizes. At the beginning of the debate we gave to the government definite principles upon which we suggested that they should proceed. I will run over them quickly: first,, the obligation to defend ourselves; second, the obligation under the united nations charter; third, efficiency; fourth, scientific development; and fifth, coordination of training and equipment with Great Britain and the United States.
I want to point out to the committee a significant matter in this debate, namely, that the minister has given us no principles whatever which have governed him in reaching any of these figures; and more than that, except possibly for the question of scientific development which he dealt with in his statement, he has not even, endorsed one of the principles which the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) laid down about . a month ago. He has not even said whether he agreed or disagreed, and he has not given us any principles of his own.
The second thing we know about the navy is this. We have been given a size in men and ships which does not jibe with efficiency. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has pointed out a rough guide of one to one; and the minister himself, in making his speech on the navy, gave some significant figures. For a force for the Pacific war bigger than the proposed peace-time fleet by some forty frigates he was going to have 13,500 at sea and a large number-I forgot what it was- of reinforcements on shore.

Thirty-five hundred.

Thirty-five hundred; and in addition to those thirty-five hundred he was going to have another 21,500 of personnel doing shore jobs during the war. That is, the relative figures between those at sea and those on shore would be one at sea to one and a half on shore. The figures he gave to-night show a proportion of five at sea to four ashore and I suggest that that does not give us any assurance that this will be an efficient navy. Although it is becoming clearer as we go on with the debate what the plans are

and I for the life of me cannot understand why we were not told in the first place all these things and so saved my talking to-night, and talking on the part of a lot of other people-we were told there was to be an interim navy; and from the suggested term and title, without any explanation, one might gather that it was not only a navy interim in personnel but a navy interim in ships. If the navy is to be interim in ships, where does that Canadian sailor's career come from? Therefore I suggest that the second consideration, the provision of a career, has not been met at all by anything that we have heard from the minister in this debate. Neither by a statement of principle nor by any statement of fact has the minister guaranteed that there will be a permanent and continuing navy which warrants a career.
Let me turn for a moment to the first consideration. The terms of service must be such as to be attractive to a young man who has the alternative of a career in civil life. The minister has given in principle terms which I find go a long way toward being satisfactory; but I suggest that October 16, some three weeks after this debate opened, was a very late time to come forward with what I should have thought would be obvious from the first, namely, that these terms of service must be laid down quickly and decisively so that men who are now making up their minds would know what to do.
Before coming to the terms of service I should like to speak for a moment on the danger of an interim navy and an indefinite policy. I suggest that indecision in this matter has an effect, first of all, on the morale of the force itself; second, on the attitude of the public toward that force, and third, on the attraction of recruit-s to the force. We all remember the pre-war attitude of this country and the great difficulty there was in obtaining recruits for a permanent force very much smaller than the proposed one. I wish to say to the minister-and this is where I take great issue with him-that we are not a warlike nation; we do not rush to the colours
[Mr. Abbott1
in peace time. We are a great country with a small population, and we have all sorts of things to do in developing this country without turning for our livelihood to the forces.
The time has come when we must maintain reasonably sized forces. The minister is now in the position where he is responsible for obtaining these men. If I were in his position I would not take my responsibility as lightly as he appears to take it. He has a very great task ahead of him and I hope he succeeds, but I suggest that he must change his attitude if he is ever to get 55,000 men for the three services.
The great problem of this government is not to decide on the particular size of the forces. The great problem of the government is to maintain interest in these services at a time when they are necessary and at a time when everybody is trying to get out of the services. As the hon. member for Vancouver South said, if he lets them go now, if he gives people the idea that he does not want them in his services, then he will have a very difficult time getting them in the spring or at any other time.
While I am on that subject may I refer to the statement of the minister that he was at present working on the demobilization programme and that there would be no recruiting campaign until early in the year. I should like to know from him to-night whether, without that recruiting campaign, and without an active recruiting campaign, we can expect to see the two cruisers in commission this winter.
The task facing the minister is not made more easy in this country by the attitude that the government took on its man-power policy during the war. The people of Canada do not believe that they handled the manpower policy any too well; and when we get this kind of thing in the peace-time services they are going to be inclined to think it is the same government with the same policy for peace time that they had in war.
I suggest that the minister must get out and get this force; I suggest that he must start as soon as he can, because I know and many other hon. members know, by talking with excellent young officers face to face who have seen service in this war, that many of them have said: "We would like to stay in; we do not know the terms of service; they are completely indefinite; we cannot wait around; we have to get out." We have had those terms of service almost dragged out in this debate like pulling teeth. I suggest to the minister that he circulate them around the country with quite as much publicity as is being given to a certain victory loan poster.

Demobilization-Naval Services
In addition to those who have said definitely that they are not going to stay in because they do not see that career ahead of them, there are any number who are undecided. Although the minister has not given us any information I hope he will do so. Any information I have had indicates that the total numbers coming forward are very small indeed. The test of it all is, of course, are those recruits coming forward in adequate numbers? Until we have that information I suppose the issue cannot be decided. But what happens to this navy if we do not get enough men? In the first place, we will never get the efficiency which it is so obvious we must have in any force. And if we do not get enough men and we want to keep up efficiency we are going to have to put ships out of commission. Fpr all we know, the Uganda is practically out of commission now at the start of the programme. We remember too that there was some desire to have a bigger navy after the last war. The cruiser Aurora in particular was kept in commission for a very short time, then taken around to Halifax and laid up, and then after everyone had forgotten about her, she was scrapped. We do not want that to happen again, and it is up to the government to make certain that it does not happen. I suggest that although the minister cannot state figures or principles, he should give us in this debate an undertaking that these ships which he has indicated will form part of the peace-time navy, will be kept in commission for a period, for as many years as he can commit himself to now. If he did that, then many fears on this side of the house and many of his difficulties in getting recruits would be removed.
I said earlier that' I thought this whole policy was one of indecision, and that there was no necessity for it. I do not want to let this opportunity pass without explaining what I meant by that. Why should we be indefinite as to the future of the navy? The minister said that because of our indefinite obligations under the united nations charter and because of the possible effect of the atomic bomb-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES

The minister said that he did not mention that. If necessary, I can refer to the passage in his speech. Certainly the Minister of National Defence for Air mentioned the atomic bomb as one of the reasons for indecision. I say that just because we have the atomic bomb, that is no reason whatever to wait before making up our minds what our forces are to be. -Ordinary forces still are necessary. We do not have to look very far back into history to see this same 47696-88
argument advanced again and again. The most recent and most striking example was just before the last war, when everyone said that the war would be decided by air power. It was quite common talk in the streets, referring to Great Britain, that we did not need an expeditionary force on the continent; it would not be of any use having one there because the war would be decided in the air. So that there was only a very small expeditionary force available to go to France in 1939, and as a result we got into all kinds of danger there. That is exactly the same argument we hear advanced now in connection with the atomic bomb; and that argument has been heard before each war all the way back through history. Therefore the atomic bomb gives us no reason for waiting, no reason not to be decisive now and know what we are going to do.
Now let us turn to our duties under the security pact of the united nations. Again there is no reason to. wait. In the first place, those duties may be undecided for an indefinite period of time, five or six years or more. What are we going to do in the meantime? In the second place, I suggest that when those duties are announced they will not affect us substantially in our calculations with respect to our armed forces. I would remind the committee of a fundamental principle in military thought, expressed in these words: every commander is responsible for his own local protection at all times. I was taught that this principle applied to a private soldier as well as to a section commander and also to a government in deciding high matters of policy. Our first duty is to defend this country to the maximum extent of which we are reasonably capable. We do not need to wait for any united nations charter to make up our minds what our defence force should be. Our duties under the security council, even when we know them and after we have provided our defence force, are not going to make much difference to us, because I suggest to the committee that our duty will consist of three things. First, we shall be. responsible for our own imfnediate local defence. Second, we shall be responsible for material aid and possibly for convoy duty in getting our materials to where the united nations want to use them. Third, it is very unlikely that we would ever be called upon for an expeditionary force, because the great powers have ample forces and they would not need a division or something like that from Canada, which would only make their administration more complicated. But even if an expeditionary force from this country were required, still that would not make any difference to the size our force

ought to be, because the use of an expeditionary force from Canada at the behest of the united nations would presuppose that the united nations were working together-
