It is always with the utmost pleasure that I listen to the remarks of my hon. friend the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt). It is the first time I have had the pleasure of rising after him, and I take this opportunity to congratulate him upon his accomplishments during the last-war. May I remind him, too, that Colonel Dollard Menard, who was with him at Dieppe, was born in my constituency. By the way, Colonel Menard, like the hon. member from Vancouver-Burrard, was not a swivel-chair hero. Both of them were good men.
I am under a handicap when discussing military matters with the hon. member who has just spoken. However, as neither of us is a sailor, we are on equal footing when we discuss naval estimates. Let me pay this tribute to the minister, that he has undertaken onerous duties. I cannot understand how he could reasonably expect to take charge of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services as well as the Department of National Defence, when they were both in such a mess. But I admire his courage, and I give him credit for assuming such responsibilities.

Demobilization-Naval Services
Coming back to the able speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, may I say. that I noted his suggestion to increase naval personnel from 10.000 to 15,000. But let us suppose that he were a young man of eligible age, without his very fine war record, and that he had thought sometimes of enlisting in the navy. After listening to a depressing speech, such as the one he has just delivered, would he have done so? No, I do not think he would have rushed to a naval recruiting office and said, "I want to become a sailor."
Of course there is poetry in a naval career. I shall always remember the sight of a young sailor who stood with his sweetheart in front of the show-case of a silversmith or jeweller. Both of them were looking at engagement rings. The sailor pointed his finger at one of them, while his fiancee looked at another. Finally, after a mild argument-an argument so mild, may I say, that we have had none of the kind in the house-the boy nodded his assent to the suggestion of the girl.
Well, there is romance! There is always romance in the navy, and because of that the navy has a special appeal. Of course there are heavy seas, and it is hard to be a sailor. At times it is a hard life, because one must remain a long time away from home. But there is so much poetry in the crests of the waves, in the music of the winds, and in the idea that one is between heaven and the sea- not between the devil and the deep blue sea-throughout all the day and all the night, for all the time. The sailor is always thinking of coming back to his home and telling his family of the wonders accomplished while the dear one was away.
There is a way to induce young men to join the navy, and there is another way to induce young men to keep far away from it. I shall leave it to the committee' to decide what the effect of the speech delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard would have been on a group of young men who, before listening to him, would have been ready to enlist in the navy.
Some proposals have been made to establish a permanent navy for the defence of this country and for the convoying of ships all over the world. One thing I do hope is that if the suggestion of the minister is accepted by the committee and by parliament, we shall have a Canadian navy which will not be under the control of the admiralty, but one which will act in cooperation with it. There is a great difference between both ideals, both suggestions.
In the first place those who believe that the Canadian navy shall be under the orders 4769G-88J
of the admiralty have an inferiority complex. They do not exist as Canadians. They do not think as Canadians. They think as human beings while living in an adjunct of the empire called Canada, and thpy still believe that the admiralty has jurisdiction over this country. There is a great difference between domination by the admiralty and cooperation with it.
I remember that when His Majesty the King came to Canada in 1939 he had on board his ship an admiral of the fleet who had that funny name of Sir Dudley Pound. Of course the ship was delayed by fog off the coast of Newfoundland, and it remained there at anchor for some time. I was very much worried, because I wanted to see the king. I said, "As a loyal Canadian subject I have a right to see the king, an3 I do not see why Dudley Pound keeps the king away from me." That was what I said in the house. Dudley Pound was there and kept the king in the fog, despite the protestations of the member for Temiscouata to let the king come ashore in this country, and land in Quebec city. But Dudley Pound was there, and Dudley Pound kept the king in the fog. Great man, Dudley Pound! But finally the king came here, and there was bright sunshine when he landed from the ship at Quebec harbour.
I met some other admirals of the fleet. In London there are at least a dozen or two admirals of the fleet. I was dumbfounded. I said to one admiral, "Who is the admiral of the fleet?" and he said, "I am". I asked again, "Who is the admiral of the fleet?" and another one answered, "I am." They were all admirals of the fleet. Here we have an admiral of the fleet called Jetty Jones. He was chosen by that great man, Angus L. Macdonald, who I hope will be defeated tomorrow, although I do hope the great Liberal party of Nova Scotia will secure a victory. Jetty Jones was not there when the explosion occurred. He was afraid of the explosion and he came here, but afterwards he was told to go back.

I admire the sailors and all members of the crews in the navy, but there is one thing I cannot understand. The men of the navy enjoy overseas preference in connection with the civil service, but the men of the merchant marine do not. These men were just as much exposed as the men in the navy but they do not get the same preference in the civil service. I cannot see any difference between the man serving on a ship under the minister and the man serving on a ship under the Minister of Transport or on the ship of some private navigation company. Stokers work under sea level in both cases and sailors run the same risks. The men in the navy who have sailed only in Canadian waters are entitled to overseas preference. I am not objecting to that, what I object to is that the man who has served on a mercantile ship does not enjoy the same overseas preference in connection with civil service appointments.
I know the minister is very well disposed toward this matter, and I know his colleagues have the same favourable disposition. But the fact is that this discrimination exists and it should be corrected at once. I know of one case-of course everything happens in my constituency-where two young men were applying for a position. One stated that he had overseas service, but the other man, who had served on a merchant ship and had gone overseas many times, did not have the same privilege. This is not fair and I am sure every member of the committee will feel likewise. It is something that should be corrected at the earliest possible opportunity.
I appreciate the kindness of the committee. I will not imitate 'Churchill in saying that I consider myself to be a child of parliament, but I consider the House of Commons is a real mother to me.

I should like to answer one or two points raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I am sorry if I conveyed the impression of being casual or of not taking my responsibilities seriously. That perhaps is

due to an unfortunate mannerism on my part, or it may be due to the fact that my hon. friend has not known me very long. I can assure him that I take my responsibilities very seriously indeed. I will express no opinion at all as to how I am discharging them, but again I assure him that I do take them very seriously.
I think the other important charge he made against me and against the government was that we had been indefinite and indecisive in announcing our post-war policy. Perhaps we have been, and I do not admit it, but I want to say that we have been more definite than any other allied country in announcing the character and composition of our post-war forces. We have been more definite than Great Britain or the United States.

My hon. friend said that we had been indefinite and had not stated in sufficient detail what our forces were to be.
I may not be able to answer that charge, but I am saying that at least we have been more definite than any other country that I know of. I think it is still too early to attempt to lay down hard and fast rules as to what those forces are to be, either as to the nature of their composition or as to their size. I never made any reference to the atomic bomb, but. I did refer to new and terrible weapons. There are a good many new weapons besides the atomic bomb, jet propulsion, for example.
I suggest that only six weeks after the end of the Japanese war is a little too early to lay down hard and fast rules as to just what types of ships we are to have or just how many men will be in our post-war forces. I think we have to proceed a little more slowly than that.

speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance moved that the house go into committee to consider this resolution to grant 81,365 million toward defraying the cost of the war and demobilization, the hon. member for Vancouver South, who opened the debate for the official opposition, outlined four broad principles which he believed should form the basis of the defence policy of this country. I propose to summarize those four principles as an introduction to my brief remarks.

Demobilization

Naval Services
Those principles are: first, that we must be prepared, if attacked, to defend Canada to the best of our ability and be in position to live up to our commitments under any agreement we enter into with the security council under the charter of the united nations. Second, we must maintain the efficiency of our armed forces. Third, our armed forces must be given the help of our scientists to enable them to keep up to date and have the most modem improvements in equipment and training. Fourth, there should be the closest coordination in training and types of equipment among the different nations of the British commonwealth and empire and the United States.
I wish to lay some emphasis this evening on the third principle that we have suggested, namely, that our armed forces have the help of our scientists. I do so because I believe that it is a matter of pressing importance. I think the minister of defence, when he made his informative statement on the navy, did not [DOT] deal with the matter fully or make a complete or wholly satisfactory statement on the subject. His remarks will be found on page 875 of Hansard, where he said:
While it may be difficult to continue naval scientific research on an extensive scale during peace time, it will be generally agreed, I think, that the service should keep itself abreast of developments in the field and that an adequate organization and facilities for that purpose must be maintained.
I would ask the minister this question: Why should it be difficult to continue scientific research on an extensive scale in peace time? I would ask him this further question:	If
we fail to continue scientific research on an extensive scale in peace time, how can we keep abreast of developments?
I want to be fair to the minister, and so . I will bring to the attention of the committee a statement he made to this house when he-spoke on Tuesday last, not as minister of national defence for the navy but as minister of defence for the army, which statement I thought was somewhat more reassuring. He said on that occasion as reported at page 1134 of Hansard:
Recent developments have demonstrated how vital it is that we should maintain an adequate organization for scientific research and development.
The desirability of placing, research on the broadest possible basis, with close integrations of the efforts of the three armed services and the national research council, is fully realized and further action to that end is now under active consideration.
Perhaps that was as far as he could go at that time for plans and policies on an important subject such as this require, time and careful consideration. But he said that active
consideration is being given to the matter, and I hope that active consideration is being given to it. The matter is of such great and urgent importance that the committee is entitled, I think to a 'complete statement of government policy in the very near future; it is entitled to this statement before this session ends. The minister told us this evening that the chief task of his department was the demobilization programme. But it seems to me that this is a task of even greater importance.
In the past, Canadian industry and government have been far too dependent on sources outside the country for the results of research and there has been little dissemination of technical knowledge. I do not think any member of the house will take issue with me on that statement. The words are not my own. They will be found in the white paper presented to parliament by the Minister of Reconstruction in April of this year, which deals with reconstruction in the second stage of the war and is entitled, "Employment and Income with Special Reference to the Initial Period of Reconstruction."
I, like many others, hold the view that scientific research has become so important that it is the vital factor in our future existence as a free country. It must be the keynote of our defence. Without it we cannot maintain our liberties against aggression. It seems to me that in view of the great discoveries and developments which have been made in the world of science during the war that has just ended, and of the future developments which we expect as a result of what we have learned, it is of the greatest importance that Canada continue its scientific investigations on an extensive scale and encourage her scientists in order that we may be in a postiion to defend our country in the days to come.
General George C. Marshall, chief of staff of the United States army, in a report he made to the secretary of war this month, on the 9th instant, urged that the United States be kept strong and ready for future aggression from any source.
For the United States to be kept in this position he recommended first and foremost "constant intensive scientific research and development." His words are as applicable to Canada as they are to the United States. If this country is to be in a position to defend itself from aggression or to wage war when its freedom is threatened the government must have constant intensive scientific research and development and close cooperation with the research organizations of Great Britain and the United States. It is, I believe, the duty

Demobilization-Naval Services
of the government to maintain and encourage scientific research in order that we can defend ourselves against modem weapons of war.
General Marshall said in his report that he had asked General H. H. Arnold, chief of the United States armed forces, to estimate the capabilities of modern weapons. General Arnold in his report referred to some of the hitherto highly secret developments, and in the course of his remarks said:
We can direct rockets to targets by electronic devices and new instruments which guide them accurately to sources of heat, light and magnetism. Drawn by their own fuses such rockets will streak unerringly to the heart of big factories, attracted by the heat of the furnaces. They are so sensitive that in the space of a large room they aim themselves towards a man wfto enters, in reaction to the heat of his body.
Within the next few years there will be produced jet-propelled bombers with speeds of 500 to 600 miles an hour, flying to targets 1,500 miles distant at altitudes above 40.000 feet. Development of even greater bombers, to operate in the stratosphere at supersonic speeds and carrying bomb loads of more than 100.000 pounds already is certain.
These aircraft will have sufficient range to attack any spot on the earth and return to a friendly base.
At this very moment we are making a single bomb weighing 45,000 pounds to keep pace with the bomber, already under construction, which will carry such a load. Air ordnance engineers have blueprinted a bomb weighing 100,000 pounds.
Improvement of jetfighters may well produce w-thin the next five years an aircraft capable of the speed of sound and of reaching targets
2,000	miles away at altitudes above 50,000 feet.
It is essential that this country, through scientific research keep pace with these developments.
General Marshall, in the course of his report, said that "discovery of the secret of atomic power can be man's greatest benefit or it can destroy him," and he added these words:
It is against the latter terrible possibility that this nation must prepare or perish.
His words are as applicable to Canada as they are to the United States. We must plan and be prepared to meet modem scientific instruments of destruction with modern scientific instruments of defence.
Last Wednesday, the 17th instant, General Marshall appeared before a congressional committee on the effect of the atomic bomb on the size of military .establishments. In the course of his evidence he said that "if a war of atomic bombs ever gets started the United States intends to have a good supply of the devastators on hand," and he went on to say that two big bomb plants were producing right now" and "building up a reserve."
What are we doing here in Canada? Have w'e or are we to have any plants that will produce these bombs? Have we any arrangement with the United States about their

production? General Marshall's statement was referred to in an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Journal the other day, which said that if these matters can be discussed openly before a congressional committee by the chief of staff of the United States army they surely can be discussed openly in parliament.
Canadian scientists have made important contributions to the development of modem weapons of war and of defence, but more important work lies ahead and should be undertaken with the assistance of the government. Constant, intensive scientific research and development should be the keystone of our defence policy.
In July of this year, Doctor Vannevar Bush, director of the office of scientific research and development, an emergency organization that has been set up in the United States, presented to the president a report dealing with what should be done to extend scientific research and development in the United States after the war. This report states that "in this war it has become clear beyond all doubt that scientific research is absolutely necessary to national security." If quotes from a joint letter which the United States secretaries of war and navy sent to the national academy of science as follows:
This war emphasizes three facts of supreme importance to national security: 1. Powerful new tactics of defence and offence are developed around new weapons created by scientific and engineering research. 2. A competitive time element in developing these weapons may be decisive 3. War is increasinly total war in which the armed services must be supplemented by active participation of every element of the civilian population.
To ensure continued preparedness along farsighted technical lines the research scientists ot the country must be called upon to continue in peace time some substantial portion of those types of contribution to the national security which they have made so effectively during the stress of the present w7ar.
The report goes on to say:
There must be more-and more adequate- military research during peace time. We cannot again rely on our allies to hold off the enemy while we struggle to catch up. Further, it is clear that only the government can undertake military research; for it must be carried on in secret. Much of it has no commercial value and is expensive. The obligation of government to support research on military problems is inescapable.
The report says that "military preparedness requires a permanent independent, civilian-controlled organization having close liaison with the army and navy but with funds directly from congress, and with clear power to initiate military research which will supplement and strengthen that carried on directly under the control of the army and the navy."	.

I quote these brief extracts from the report as it appears in the appendix to Fortune magazine of September, since they support the position I have taken, and I would suggest to the minister that he and his officials make a study of the report if they have not already done so.	.
I would now ask the minister to tell us what the government proposes to do with the mechanical and engineering buildings of the national defence council which were erected near the city of Ottawa early in the war, at, I understand, at a cost of $3 millions. Is it the intention of the government to keep these buildings open and functioning as at present? Does it propose to keep up the staffs of scientific workers in these buildings ^ or to curtail the staffs? If it proposes to curtail them, to what extent? Has it lost any of the scientists who were employed in those buildings since peace was declared, or perhaps I should say more correctly, since the termination of hostilities.
There is another matter that I would refer to briefly. It has to do with the conversion of our industries from peace to a war basis in the event of hostilities. I do not think this matter has been referred to in this debate. In making plans for our future defence consideration should be given to a tie-in with industry and close planning so that quick industrial mobilization may be had in the event of war in order that there may be a quick turnover from peace to war production. This should be a matter of close study by the government in cooperation with our industrialists and the plans that are drawn up should be reviewed from time to time.
We all know how difficult and disquieting was the process of developing war industries and turning out the necessary munitions of war after we declared war in 1939. We all know of the difficulties and delays we experienced then in obtaining plants, machine tools, materials and equipment, and what great delays there were at that time. What we learned as a result of that experience should not be lightly brushed aside or forgotten, but we should profit by those rather bitter lessons. They should be made the basis for future defence in planning the conversion of peacetime industries in the event of war and also in connection with the reserves of essential materials. Has this matter been given consideration by the government? It is a matter that should have its best consideration as I have already said, and plans should be made in order that our peace-time industries may be turned over to war-time industries as quickly as possible in the event of hostilities.
In conclusion, I desire to say that I believe the defence of our country is one of such vital importance that it should not become a matter of party politics. It should be placed on a level above party. Never again should there be any cleavage on the size or effectiveness of our armed forces. This may be a difficult thing to bring about; it may be difficult to prevent such a cleavage from happening. Undoubtedly there will be differences of opinion, but those differences of opinion should not develop into party issues if this can be avoided. It would assist in preventing this from happening if a standing committee of the house were set up by the government on defence matters as we have suggested. This committee would enable members of the house to obtain first hand information from chiefs of staffs and other experts, which would be not only of great educational value but also of great value in enabling them to come to sound conclusions on defence policies that are so vital to the future safety of this nation.

maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext: That has happened on several occasions this session. We want to get down to serious business. We want to discuss the affairs of the government of this country. We do not expect that every time we ask questions somebody will rise to give a jocular speech.

maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext:
I mentioned before that recently I was in the naval hospital at Halifax. The people of Canada have reason to be proud of the splendid medical and hospital services being provided for the men in that hospital. One young man from my constituency who was in the hospital is now back in Saskatchewan where we have not- the same medical and hospital services available that were available in the service. I draw the minister's attention to the'report of a national health survey conducted by the medical procurement and assignment board. The next time the committee meets I wonder if he will let us know the number of medical officers now in the navy as compared with the navy personnel, and also the figures for the army and the air force.
When this committee report was brought down we had a ratio of 4-9 medical men per thousand of men. in the navy; 4-5 for the army and 3-66 for the air force. The committee suggested that a rate of between 3-5 and 3-7 per thousand should be ample for all medical needs. I think everyone is agreed that in the midst of war the very best services should be provided, but now that the war is over I think we might expect that progress might be made in reducing these ratios.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext:
I shall try to get that
information. There were just one or two points raised by the hon. member for York South. He asked when the estimates were prepared. The first estimates were prepared last spring, when estimates are always prepared. They have been revised and revised, the final revision, so far as my final approval was concerned, having occurred on September 5. I think we called it a day when the session opened, and at that time the Japanese war was over.

maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext: You have let out many more men since that time than you anticipated.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext:
About what we anticipated. At the time of the final revision we contemplated a discharge rate of about 10,000 a month. I do not want to appear to be in a jocular vein, and I have not put up the hon.
fMr. Cockeram.]
member for Temiscouata or any one else to answer for me. I intend to do that myself. When I answered the 'hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard I did not intend to introduce any jocular tone into the discussion. I am here to answer any questions hon. members want to ask and I shall try to do so to the best of my ability.

maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext: What about those articles that appeared in the periodical News?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext: I am prepared to make a full statement on that, but it is a little late to do so to-night. The articles related to certain yachts that were taken over and to the developments at Shelbourne. I shall be delighted to give a full statement in answer to the article by Mr. Carr.

maintopic: I3S6 COMMONS
speechtext:
The United States
Secretary of the Navy Forrestal, in making a report to congress recently, stated that the function of the United States navy was to take the war to the enemy and that, despite the new and devastating weapons, there could be very little change in the classical functions of the navy. He supported his contention by requesting a great increase in the scientific work and specialized training being done by officers of the- United States navy.
That brings me to the question I want to ask about Royal Roads. I do not know whether the minister has seen the announcement recently made that the United Kingdom does not intend to keep open Woolwich academy. In other words, the Shop is to be closed. That seems to be an extraordinary decision to have been taken, to close this highly technical training establishment in the United Kingdom.
I do not suppose there is any service where the permanent officers must be as highly skilled and must undergo such a lengthy, rigorous and constant training as the regular naval officer. He is taken as a boy in his middle teens and educated for probably three or four years in the naval college. He then becomes a midshipman and goes on for probably another two years. In Royal Roads we have an excellent training establishment, situated where training can be carried on for twelve months in the year. It is situated on an excellent bay; it is well established, and in my opinion it is extremely well run. That was my opinion when I visited it some months ago.
In view of the uncertainties that must be set many of the services I think we should have a fairly definite statement upon this matter. It takes a long time to train a permanent naval officer. He is a highly skilled

Demobilization-Naval Services
technician; as new weapons are perfected he will become more and more highly skilled and his training will have to be more and more intense. We must induce the right type of young Canadian to go into the naval service.
This war has shown, as nothing else has, that the Canadian has a peculiar genius for naval service. The traditions of the British navy have been well identified and carried on by the Canadian navy. If we are to fulfil our duties toward ourselves and the united nations we must see to it that the permanent officers taken into the navy are keen and anxious and willing. Every year there are a great number of men who want to get into the naval services. In view of that I am going to ask the minister this question concerning Royal Roads. Will the Royal Naval College at Royal Roads be continued? The second question is: Will there be any changes in the scope or length of the course contemplated? The third question is: In view of the development in the size of our army from its small pre-war establishment will the number of cadets admitted annually to Royal Roads be increased?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

Perhaps my hon. friend would allow me to answer those questions . the first thing when the committee resumes. My reason for asking that is that the acting leader of the house would like to have the committee rise and report progress in order to get two departments into supply. I can answer the first question now. Royal Roads will continue.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday evening I said that I would like the permission of the house to move two departments into supply on civil estimates, just to call them, not for consideration of the items.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Might I ask the reason for the urgency? As I understand it, we have the estimates of all three services before us in committee already without a single item having been passed. What, then, is the urgency for putting two more departments into supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
It has been the custom ever since I have been in the house to ask for permission to move not too many but at least five or six departments into supply on civil estimates so that they may be considered when other business is not available for consideration by members of the house. There
is no urgency in the matter. It is just a matter of convenience. If the house is opposed I shall not1 press the matter at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Why not bring in four departments instead of just two?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: After the motion in regard to Wednesday sitting is carried there will only be two days on which a motion for supply can be moved, when any hon. member has the privilege of bringing up any grievance that he wishes to have redressed. There are about twenty departments altogether to be moved into supply, so that ample opportunity will be afforded to any hon. member to voice any complaint or move for the redressing of any grievance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: So long as we have about sixteen other departments on which to talk about our grievances, we will agree.

I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that there are two parts to this amendment, and that they stand together. The two parts are, first of all, a request for the immediate appointment of a government controller, and, second, the enactment of certain legislation. When I say that the two parts stand together I am underlining the fact that it would not really solve the situation just to appoint a government controller. That could be done and the result might be the forcing of the employees back to work without any satisfactory settlement of the dispute for a long period of time. I point out that concurrent with the appoint-men of a controller there is required the enactment of legislation that strikes at the root of the trouble. The employees at the Ford plant are asking what we believe to be one of the things the war itself was fought for, namely, industrial democracy. They are asking that the union at Windsor be given the same amount of union security that is enjoyed by their fellow workers in (he Ford plants across the river in Detroit.
